title: The beat of the sentence: which words carry it and which almost vanish

fields.examples_en:
She was born in the north of England.
What do you want to do at the weekend?
We could have gone to the beach, but it rained.
fields.excerpt: Content words carry the rhythm of spoken English; the grammar words between them shrink to fit.
fields.explanation: Spoken English does not give every word equal weight. In the model sentence, only four words are pronounced in full: the verb, the noun that follows it, and the two words that measure the time at the end. These are the content words - they carry the information, and they carry the beat. Everything between them - the auxiliaries, the articles, the two identical prepositions - is squeezed into brief unstressed syllables, most reduced to the neutral vowel. The stressed words arrive at roughly even intervals, and the grammar words compress to fit the space between beats. This is not lazy or casual speech: it is the normal rhythm of the language at every level of formality.
fields.next_label: Next: how the beat inside a single word can move and change its meaning
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: I've been waiting for a bus for half an hour.
fields.watch_out: Learners taught from the written page give every word its full dictionary pronunciation, and the damage runs in both directions. Spoken that way, a sentence sounds mechanical, because the rhythm a native listener uses to locate the important words is flattened away. Worse, the same habit ruins listening: if you expect the auxiliaries and prepositions to sound as they do in isolation, you will listen for full forms that never arrive, decide that native speakers swallow most of their words, and blame the speed. The speed is not the problem. What sounds like missing words is the set of weak forms - and once you listen for a compressed neutral vowel instead of the citation form, whole stretches of natural speech become audible.

title: The consonant at the end of a word carries the grammar

fields.examples_en:
She lives near the park and walks there every day.
They watched the match and then washed the cups.
My son wants two tickets, not one ticket.
fields.excerpt: Plural, past and third person all live in the final consonant, so dropping it drops the grammar.
fields.explanation: English words very often end in a consonant, and a great deal of the grammar is carried there. The ending that marks a plural noun, the ending that marks a finished action and the ending that marks a present verb with a third-person subject are, in the ordinary case, a single consonant fastened to the end of the word; only after a few particular sounds does one of them take a small vowel of its own and add a whole syllable. They are never stressed, but they are pronounced. English also allows two or more consonants to close a syllable together, with no vowel between them and none after the last of them. A word does not stop at the vowel unless the spelling says it does.
fields.next_label: Next: the ending a verb takes when the subject is somebody else
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: My friend works in two shops and she helped me last week.
fields.watch_out: Speakers of languages whose syllables normally end in a vowel do one of two things here, and both are damaging. Some let the final consonant disappear altogether. Others keep it but add a small vowel after it, turning one syllable into two and making the word unrecognisable. Either way the listener stops receiving the grammatical endings, and three systems fail at the same moment: number, past time, and the present form used with a third-person subject. The error is tempting because those endings are unstressed and genuinely quiet in fluent speech, so they seem optional; and since the learner writes them correctly and knows the rule, they are sure they have said them. Record yourself and listen to the last sound of every word.

title: Punctual, or early enough? Two expressions that are not interchangeable

fields.examples_en:
She handed the report in on time, which surprised everyone.
We got to the airport in time to have a coffee before boarding.
The bus was not on time, but we still arrived in time for the film.
fields.excerpt: One small word separates arriving punctually from arriving with time to spare.
fields.explanation: These two expressions differ by one small word and mean genuinely different things, and the model sentence uses both so that the contrast is visible in a single breath. One of them means punctual: the event happened at the moment it was scheduled to happen, and the reference point is a timetable, an appointment or a promise. The other means early enough: something was accomplished before a deadline closed, with room to spare, and the reference point is whatever had to be done afterwards. The first is a judgement about a schedule; the second is a judgement about a consequence.
fields.next_label: Next: the full scale behind these three small words
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: The train arrived on time, so we were in time to catch our connection.
fields.watch_out: The third example sentence is the one to study, because it uses both expressions about the same journey and they do not contradict each other. The vehicle failed the schedule, so the first expression is negated; the travellers still beat the deadline that mattered, so the second holds. Learners who treat the two as interchangeable produce sentences that are grammatical but say the wrong thing, and in a work context the difference is not cosmetic: telling a manager that a report was delivered punctually makes a claim about the agreed date, while telling them it was delivered early enough makes a claim about the deadline it had to beat, and only one of those may be true.

title: The sound that decides which form goes in front

fields.examples_en:
She waited an hour for an honest answer.
He is studying for a university degree and a European qualification.
They gave me an MBA prospectus and a one-page summary.
fields.excerpt: The article in front of a noun is chosen by the first sound you hear, never by the first letter.
fields.explanation: The indefinite article has two written forms, and the choice between them is settled by the first sound of the next word, never by its first letter. One form is used when that word begins with a consonant sound, the other when it begins with a vowel sound. Because English spelling and English pronunciation drifted apart centuries ago, the letter and the sound frequently disagree, and it is always the sound that wins. Say the following word quietly to yourself before choosing, and the rule never fails you.
fields.next_label: Next: the table showing all four choices, including using nothing
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: It takes an hour to reach a university on the far side of the city.
fields.watch_out: The trap catches careful learners rather than careless ones, because a careful learner looks at the written word. In the first example sentence both nouns open with a consonant letter that is silent, so the first sound is a vowel and the longer form is required. In the second sentence both nouns open with a vowel letter but are pronounced beginning with the gliding consonant made by raising the tongue towards the roof of the mouth, so the shorter form is required. The third sentence shows both traps at once: an abbreviation whose first letter is a consonant but is read aloud as its name, which starts with a vowel, and a number word beginning with a vowel letter but pronounced with a rounded-lip consonant at the front.

title: The four parts of a strong interview answer, and what weakens it

fields.examples_en:
In my last job I managed a team of six, and I cut our monthly reporting time from three days to one.
I had never used that software, so I taught myself over a weekend and trained two colleagues the following month.
I would like to be leading a small team within three years, which is one reason this role interests me.
fields.excerpt: A good interview answer is a tiny story in four fixed parts, and most weak answers skip one of them.
fields.explanation: A strong answer to a question about your experience is a very small story, and it has four parts in a fixed order: the situation and when it arose, the difficulty inside it, what you personally did about it, and what changed as a result. The model sentence above does all four in one breath. Notice how little of it describes your character: it fixes a moment on the calendar, names one difficulty, gives one action with a first-person subject, and ends on an outcome anyone could check. Interviewers are trained to listen for that last part, and it is the part candidates most often leave out, stopping instead at the point where the effort was made.
fields.next_label: Next: the two-part verbs to swap for a single formal verb when you want to sound measured
fields.subject: business
fields.target_en: When a supplier missed a deadline last March, I rebuilt the delivery schedule in two days and we shipped on time.
fields.watch_out: The weak version of any of these answers is not wrong English; it is English with the evidence taken out. Look at what each of the three example sentences carries: a pair of figures, a stretch of time, or a horizon you could be held to. Remove those and the same grammar produces sentences anyone could say about any job. Two habits do the removing. The first is reaching for adjectives about your own character instead of one episode, because adjectives are far easier to produce under pressure in a foreign language than a narrative is. The second is the plural subject: in many workplaces claiming personal credit feels impolite, so candidates report what the group achieved and the interviewer never learns what they did themselves.

title: Two sounds from one spelling, and the wrong ones learners reach for

fields.examples_en:
These are my mother and father, and that is their other brother.
I think both paths are worth something.
They both thought the third answer was the truth.
fields.excerpt: One pair of letters spells two different consonants, and every substitute learners reach for is already a real word.
fields.explanation: One letter pair spells two different consonants here, and English gives no spelling clue about which one you are looking at. Both are made in the same place: the tip of the tongue rests lightly against the edge of the upper front teeth and air is pushed through the narrow gap. The airflow is never shut off and never released as a burst, so it simply keeps running. The only difference between the two is voice. In one, the vocal cords stay still and you hear plain escaping air. In the other they vibrate, and a finger on your throat will feel it. The model sentence above contains seven of them: two voiced, five voiceless.
fields.next_label: Next: the letters English writes down but never actually says
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: My brother thinks these three things are worth nothing.
fields.watch_out: The sound is rarely dropped. Learners replace it with the nearest neighbour their own language offers, and which one they reach for depends on that language. Many French, German and Slavic speakers pull the tongue back behind the teeth and produce a hiss or a buzz, which turns the last noun of the third example sentence into an unrelated word. Russian, Thai and many other Asian speakers close the gap and make a hard stop. Some urban British and Caribbean speakers move the contact forward to the lower lip and upper teeth. Each substitute is an ordinary English consonant, so the result is not an accent but a different word. Fix the mouth first: tongue tip between the teeth, air still moving, and only then decide whether the throat buzzes.

title: The small second word that decides what a verb means

fields.examples_en:
She puts on a warm coat before she goes outside.
Please sit down while I turn off the television.
He is looking for his keys under the newspapers.
fields.excerpt: The two-part verbs a beginner meets in the very first week, and why the small word that follows the verb is never decoration.
fields.explanation: Each expression here is an ordinary verb followed by one small word - a particle, which is either an adverb or a preposition. The two words work as a single unit, and the small one carries much of the meaning. In the model sentence the first verb, used alone, would mean to obtain or receive something; with its particle it means to leave your bed. The second verb, used alone, would mean to rotate; with its particle it means to make a machine start working. Nothing in the verbs themselves predicts this. That is why such pairs are learnt as single items of vocabulary, exactly as you would learn any new word, and why they fill ordinary conversation.
fields.next_label: Next: where the small word goes once the sentence has an object
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.target_en: Every morning I get up at six, turn on the radio and look for my shoes.
fields.watch_out: The error to guard against is treating the small word as decoration and leaving it out - a habit of learners whose own language expresses the whole idea with a single verb. Stripped of its particle, the last verb in the model sentence means only to direct your eyes somewhere; it says nothing about searching. Replace that particle with another and the sense shifts again, to watching something happen, or to taking care of a person or an animal. The trap runs the other way with the machine verb in the middle: the two opposite particles it takes are the only thing separating starting the device from stopping it, so the wrong choice reverses your meaning while the sentence still sounds perfectly natural.

title: Why a friendly opening sounds wrong in a formal setting

fields.examples_en:
Good afternoon, my name is Tomas Reyes and I have an appointment with Dr Hall.
Good morning, my name is Lena Fischer and I am here to see the manager.
Good evening, my name is Sam Okoye and I have a table for eight o'clock.
fields.excerpt: Every greeting also announces how close you think you are to the other person, which is why a warm one can misfire.
fields.explanation: Every English greeting carries a second message underneath the first. On the surface it says you have noticed the other person; underneath it announces how close you believe the two of you are. In a room where you have met nobody yet, a reception desk, a job interview, a first day, you have no standing to announce closeness, so the safe choice is the neutral, slightly long opening: the time-of-day form, your full name, and the reason you are there. The model sentence does all three in one breath, which is why it survives almost any formal room.
fields.next_label: Next: the same choice of register, made in writing at the top of an email
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.target_en: Good morning, I'm Ana Ruiz and I have an interview with Mrs Hale at ten.
fields.watch_out: The error is opening a formal encounter with a street greeting: the short casual question friends toss at each other in passing, the one with a rising tone that nobody actually answers. It is tempting for an honest reason, because it is the form learners hear most in films and songs, so it feels like the warm, natural choice. At a reception desk it is not heard as warm; it is heard as someone who has not noticed where they are standing, and the person behind the desk quietly adjusts their expectations. The opposite slip costs less but still lands oddly: the full three-part introduction from the model sentence, delivered to people who already know you, sounds stiff, and can even be heard as teasing. Choose for the room, not for your mood.

title: Idioms you must learn whole

fields.examples_en:
She broke the ice with a joke as soon as she walked in.
They kept me in the dark about the merger for weeks.
We had to make ends meet on one salary that year.
fields.excerpt: Fixed expressions behave like single vocabulary items: their verb bends into any tense, while every other word is locked and no synonym may be substituted.
fields.explanation: A fixed expression works like a single item of vocabulary, not like a sentence you assemble word by word. Only the verb carrying the tense is free: it inflects for whatever tense and person the context needs, exactly as it would anywhere else, and if the expression leaves an open slot for a person, any person can fill it. Everything else is frozen - the nouns, their articles, any second verb, the prepositions and the singular or plural choice are all part of the stored item and cannot be edited. Replace one of those locked words with a synonym meaning precisely the same thing and the expression stops working; a listener then hears a literal statement instead.
fields.next_label: Next: a fixed expression for refusing to choose a side
fields.subject: idioms
fields.target_en: He let the cat out of the bag before the party had even started.
fields.watch_out: Two habits give a learner away here. The first is reaching for a synonym: in the opening sentence, both the animal and the container it escapes from feel replaceable, since a dictionary offers two or three equivalents for each - but any substitution turns the line literal and the meaning vanishes. The second is adjusting the number: the frozen noun in the third example sentence is plural and stays plural whatever the subject, while the frozen noun in the first example sentence is singular and keeps its article every time. Only the second example sentence has a genuinely open slot, the person left uninformed, and that slot changes freely while the fixed words around it never do.

title: Reporting a claim without owning it

fields.examples_en:
The company is said to have known about the fault for months.
There is thought to be little appetite for another restructuring.
Senior staff are understood to be resisting the proposal.
It has long been alleged that the figures were adjusted.
fields.excerpt: How formal written English lets you pass on what people are claiming while quietly making clear that you are not the one claiming it.
fields.explanation: These structures let you transmit a claim to your reader while declining to endorse it. The passive removes the source, so nobody is named as the person making the claim and you take on no responsibility for whether it is true. Two shapes carry this: a dummy subject followed by a passive reporting verb and a full clause; and a raised subject, meaning the person or thing the claim is about, or the existential opener standing in the same slot, followed by a passive reporting verb and an infinitive. Use the simple infinitive when the reported situation overlaps with the reporting or is still to come, and the perfect infinitive when it was already over before the reporting.
fields.next_label: Practice: shift the verb back when you report a statement
fields.subject: business
fields.target_en: It is widely assumed that the merger will proceed.
fields.watch_out: The subject at the front of the second pattern belongs to the reported event, not to the act of reporting: that person or company is not saying anything, other people are saying it about them. Learners routinely build the sentence as though the named subject were the one reporting, which reverses the meaning entirely. Second, choose the infinitive by time rather than by the tense of the reporting verb: the simple form for a situation that still holds or has yet to happen, the perfect form for one that was already finished. Third, remember what the register costs you. These structures are cold and institutional, and in a spoken meeting they read as evasion rather than as care, so a named source is usually stronger when you have one.

title: The opening phrase that describes the wrong person

fields.examples_en:
Walking to the station, I got caught in the rain.
As I was walking to the station, the rain started.
Having checked the figures again, the auditors withdrew their objection.
Once the figures had been checked, the objection was withdrawn.
fields.excerpt: A phrase at the start of a sentence quietly borrows its subject from the main clause, which is how confident writers end up attributing an action to whatever happens to follow the comma.
fields.explanation: An opening phrase built on a verb form has no subject of its own. It borrows one automatically from the main clause that follows, whoever or whatever that subject happens to be. So when the main clause names something that did not perform the action in the opener, the sentence claims something absurd, and it does so with flawless grammar and no warning signal. There are exactly two repairs: make the real doer the subject of the main clause, or expand the opening phrase into a full clause with a subject of its own.
fields.next_label: Reference: more traps that fluent writers fall into
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: Having reviewed your file, we have issued a refund.
fields.watch_out: This is not a learner error but a fluent-writer error, and it is everywhere in business email. It appears most often when the opener describes something a person did and the main clause is passive, so the only subject on offer is a document, a payment or a decision. Readers normally reconstruct the intended meaning, which is why the habit survives unchallenged, but for a moment the sentence says something ridiculous and attentive readers do notice. Compare the repairs above: the first and third lines supply the real doer as the subject of the main clause, while the second and fourth give the opening phrase a subject of its own. If neither repair is available to you, the shortened opener is simply the wrong structure for that sentence.

title: Granting your opponent a point, then taking it back

fields.examples_en:
For all its charm, the proposal is unworkable.
Try as he might, he never persuaded the committee.
Much as we would like to help, our funding ends in April.
Painful as the reorganisation was, it saved the department.
fields.excerpt: A set of frozen openings that let you concede the other side's point in the first half of the sentence so that your own argument lands with full weight in the second.
fields.explanation: English can grant the opposing point first, in a marked opening placed before the main clause, so that the argument you actually want to make arrives last and therefore lands hardest. Three frozen frames do this work: one built on an adverb of degree plus the linking word and a clause, normally with a verb of liking or admiring inside it; one built on a preposition plus a noun phrase naming the quality you are conceding; and one that pulls a single adjective, or the bare form of a verb, to the front of the clause before that same linking word. The order inside each frame is fixed, nothing may be inserted into it, and the parts cannot be reordered. Everything after the comma is the real point of the sentence.
fields.next_label: Practice: rebuild sentences that begin with a marked opening
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: Much as I admire her energy, I cannot support the plan.
fields.watch_out: The usual trap is reaching for the ordinary concessive conjunction instead. That version is perfectly correct, but it flattens the sentence: the marked opening is precisely what signals that you have weighed the other side and are still ruling against it. The second trap is fronting the wrong element. In the second and fourth lines a single word moves to the front, the bare form of the verb or the adjective on its own, and it sits immediately before the linking word with the subject following in normal order. Do not swap the subject and the verb after that linking word, because a question-like order there is wrong. Note also that the frame in the second line is not finished at the subject: it needs the modal that follows, and without it the sentence collapses.

title: Saying that something exists

fields.examples_en:
There is a small café on the corner.
There are three bedrooms in the flat.
There is some milk in the fridge.
There are a lot of tourists here in summer.
fields.excerpt: How English announces that something exists, and how the noun that follows chooses between the two openers.
fields.explanation: To say that something exists or is present in a place, English opens the sentence with a special two-word opener instead of the thing itself. The opener has a singular form and a plural form: the first goes before one thing, the second before several. The real subject comes after the verb, so the noun that follows decides which form you need.
fields.next_label: Practise choosing the right opener
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: There is a supermarket near my house, and there are two banks on the same street.
fields.watch_out: Many languages announce existence with a verb of possession, and translating that word for word produces a sentence English speakers never say. Remember too that uncountable nouns take the singular opener, even when the amount feels large.

title: Where the little word goes in two-part verbs

fields.examples_en:
She picked the keys up and put them in her bag.
Can you fill in this form and hand it in by Friday?
I'll look after your plants while you're away.
He turned the offer down without even reading it.
fields.excerpt: Where the object goes in two-part verbs - and the one position a pronoun is never allowed to take.
fields.explanation: A separable phrasal verb lets its object sit in two places: after the particle, or between the verb and the particle. With a noun object, both orders are correct. With a pronoun object there is no choice at all - the pronoun must go between the two parts, never after the particle. Inseparable phrasal verbs are the mirror image: their object always follows the particle, whatever kind of word it is.
fields.next_label: Practise placing the small words
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.target_en: Please turn off the television - or just turn it off at the wall.
fields.watch_out: The mistake that marks a learner instantly is placing a pronoun after the particle. Nouns give you a free choice; pronouns never do. And do not try to split an inseparable verb - its two parts work as a single word and cannot be pulled apart.

title: How the verb steps back when you pass on someone's words

fields.examples_en:
He said he was working late that night.
They told me they had already seen the film.
She promised she would send the report before Friday.
My neighbour mentioned that he was moving out the following month.
fields.excerpt: What happens to tenses, pronouns and time expressions when you pass on yesterday's words today.
fields.explanation: After a past reporting verb, the tense inside the reported clause moves one step back: a present form becomes past, a simple past becomes the past perfect, and the future auxiliary changes to its past-time form. This happens because the whole report is now anchored to a past moment of speaking. Pronouns adjust to the reporter's point of view, and time expressions tied to the original moment shift to their more distant equivalents.
fields.next_label: Practise shifting the verb back
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: She said she was tired and would call me the next day.
fields.watch_out: Two things resist the shift: past modal forms have no further step back and stay as they are, and a reported fact that is still true now may keep its original tense. The commonest real-world error, though, is shifting the verb but forgetting to move the pronouns and time expressions with it, so the report contradicts itself.

title: The small letter that changes the verb when someone else acts

fields.examples_en:
My brother plays football every weekend.
The bus leaves at eight o'clock.
I play tennis, but my sister plays better.
It rains a lot here in June.
fields.excerpt: Why the verb gains one small letter when the subject is a single other person or thing - and nowhere else.
fields.explanation: In the present simple, the verb changes for only one group of subjects: a single person or thing other than you and me. For those subjects the verb takes the -s ending; with every other subject it keeps its base form. It is one small letter, but listeners notice immediately when it is missing.
fields.next_label: Practise choosing the right present ending
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: She works in a hospital.
fields.watch_out: Negatives and questions already carry the ending inside the helper verb, so the main verb goes back to its base form there. Learners often mark it twice - once on the helper and again on the main verb. Put it on the helper only.

title: Asking for things politely in work emails

fields.examples_en:
Could you confirm the meeting time by Thursday?
Would you mind checking the figures once more before we send them?
I was wondering if you could forward me the client's feedback.
Please let me know if you need anything else from my side.
fields.excerpt: Why direct commands fail in work emails, and which softening frames native writers use instead.
fields.explanation: In written workplace English, a bare command form reads as cold or even rude, however friendly you feel. Politeness is built with softening frames: a modal question wrapped around the base verb, a fixed frame that takes the -ing form, or an indirect opener that presents the request as a gentle enquiry. The longer and more indirect the frame, the more polite it sounds - and written requests need more softening than spoken ones, because the reader cannot hear a warm voice.
fields.next_label: Ready-made lines for opening and closing an email
fields.subject: business
fields.target_en: Could you send me the updated file when you have a moment?
fields.watch_out: Two traps. First, the frame that takes the -ing form works in reverse: agreeing to help means answering negatively, because the question literally asks whether the task bothers you. Second, attaching a courtesy word to a bare command does not neutralise it in writing - the reader still sees an order.

title: The regular way to talk about finished actions

fields.examples_en:
We visited my grandparents last weekend.
The match finished at ten o'clock.
She stopped the car and opened the door.
I studied French for three years at school.
fields.excerpt: One ending turns a regular verb into the past - when to use it, and how the spelling shifts along the way.
fields.explanation: Regular verbs mark a finished past action with a single ending, the -ed form, and the same form works for every subject. Use it when the action is over and the time is stated or clear from context - yesterday, last week, in 2019. The spelling adjusts in two common cases: a short verb ending in one vowel plus one consonant doubles that consonant, and a verb ending in a consonant plus the letter y changes the y to i before the ending.
fields.next_label: Practise building the regular past
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: Last night I watched a film and then studied for two hours.
fields.watch_out: In negatives and questions, the past marking moves onto the helper verb, so the main verb goes back to its base form - keeping the past ending on both is the classic error at this level. Watch the spelling traps too: the doubling and the letter change happen only in their exact cases, not everywhere.

title: Rewriting the question in your own words

fields.examples_en:
It is often argued that advertising aimed at children does more harm than good.
Whether governments should fund space exploration remains a controversial question.
In recent years, the way we shop has been transformed almost beyond recognition by online retail.
fields.excerpt: How to reword an essay prompt so the examiner sees your language, not the question's.
fields.explanation: Examiners read your first sentence to see whether you can rework the prompt, and copied wording earns nothing - in IELTS and Cambridge marking, lifted phrases are ignored when your language is assessed. Rewrite the prompt in three ways at once: swap key words for synonyms, change word forms so a verb becomes a noun or an adjective becomes an adverb, and reorder the sentence structure so it no longer mirrors the original. The meaning must stay identical; only the wording changes.
fields.next_label: Connectors that hold an essay together
fields.subject: exams
fields.target_en: Whether children benefit more from classroom teaching or from learning online has become a matter of real debate.
fields.watch_out: The danger is over-paraphrasing: reaching for a rare synonym that shifts the meaning or does not fit the context, which costs more marks than the copying you were trying to avoid. Two or three well-chosen substitutions plus a new sentence shape are enough - and technical or topic words with no natural synonym should stay exactly as they are.

title: When the stress moves, the meaning changes

fields.examples_en:
Exports increased sharply last year.
The country exports most of its coffee.
She gave me a lovely present.
They will present the results on Monday.
fields.excerpt: How moving the stress from one syllable to the other turns a thing into an action in dozens of common word pairs.
fields.explanation: A whole family of two-syllable words works as both noun and verb, and stress is what tells them apart: the noun stresses the first syllable, the verb stresses the second. The vowels change with the stress, because the unstressed syllable weakens, so the two versions genuinely sound different - not just louder in different places. When you meet a word of this type, learn it as two spoken words that happen to share one spelling.
fields.next_label: Another pronunciation trap: three sounds for one written past ending
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: We need to record the meeting so everyone has a record of the decisions.
fields.watch_out: Learners tend to pick one stress pattern per spelling and use it everywhere, usually the noun pattern. Stressing the wrong syllable does more damage than a wrong vowel - listeners often hear a different word, or nothing recognisable at all. When in doubt, apply the rough rule: first syllable for the thing, second syllable for the action.

title: Starting with a negative for dramatic effect

fields.examples_en:
Rarely do we see a government admit its mistakes so openly.
Under no circumstances should passengers open the doors themselves.
Never in my life have I heard such nonsense.
Not once did he apologise for the delay.
fields.excerpt: The formal word-order swap that follows a fronted negative phrase, and why it makes writing sound emphatic.
fields.explanation: When a negative or restrictive adverbial opens the sentence for emphasis, the subject and the auxiliary swap places, exactly as they would in a question. If the verb has no auxiliary of its own, the dummy auxiliary steps in to carry the tense and the main verb returns to its base form. The inversion applies only in the clause the fronted phrase introduces; the rest of the sentence keeps normal word order. The effect is formal and dramatic, at home in speeches, formal writing and literary prose.
fields.next_label: Practise dramatic negative openings
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: Not only did the company miss its targets, but it also lost its two biggest clients.
fields.watch_out: The first trap is halfway inversion: fronting the negative phrase but leaving subject and verb in normal order, which reads as a plain error rather than emphasis. The second is forgetting the dummy auxiliary when the verb is a simple present or past - those forms have no auxiliary of their own to move, so one must be supplied.

title: Two everyday verbs learners constantly mix up

fields.examples_en:
Sorry, I can't come out tonight - I have to do my homework.
He made dinner for the whole family on Sunday.
Stop making so much noise; I'm trying to do some work.
We need to make a decision before Friday.
fields.excerpt: Two everyday verbs share the work that a single verb does in most other languages - here is how English splits it.
fields.explanation: English divides everyday actions between two all-purpose verbs, and the noun decides which one you need. The first verb in the model sentence pairs with results that come into existence: errors, meals, plans, promises, noise. The second pairs with activities and duties you carry out: schoolwork, housework, the shopping, your best effort. There is no logic to reason out in the moment - learn each noun together with its verb, as one chunk.
fields.next_label: Practise picking the right all-purpose verb
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.target_en: I made a big mistake yesterday, so today I'm doing the whole exercise again.
fields.watch_out: Most languages cover both of these verbs with a single word, so learners pick one English verb and use it everywhere - usually the wrong one, because the activity verb feels more general. No rule will rescue you mid-sentence: the pairings are fixed by habit, and the only safe method is memorising noun and verb as a single unit.

title: Real future possibilities and their results

fields.examples_en:
If you finish early, we can go for a coffee.
She will miss the train if she doesn't leave now.
If the weather is nice on Saturday, they'll have the party in the garden.
fields.excerpt: How English links a real future possibility to its result, and why one half of the sentence stays in the present.
fields.explanation: The first conditional describes a real future possibility and its result. The condition clause, introduced by the conditional conjunction, stays in the present simple even though its meaning is future; the result clause takes the future auxiliary plus the base form of the verb. The two clauses can come in either order - when the condition comes first, a comma separates them; when it comes second, no comma is needed.
fields.next_label: Practise real conditions and results
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
fields.watch_out: The strongest pull is to put the future auxiliary in both halves of the sentence, because many languages do exactly that. In English the condition clause never takes it - the present simple there already points to the future. Only the result clause carries the future marking.

title: Three different sounds for one written ending

fields.examples_en:
I washed the dishes and cooked dinner.
She opened the window and listened to the rain.
They wanted to stay, but we needed to leave.
He worked all weekend and finished the project.
fields.excerpt: One written past ending, three spoken sounds - and the simple rule your mouth already wants to follow.
fields.explanation: The regular past ending is written one way but spoken three ways, and the last sound of the verb decides which. After a voiceless sound - one made without the vocal cords vibrating - the ending is a short /t/. After a voiced sound, including all vowels, it is a short /d/. Only when the verb itself already ends in a /t/ or /d/ sound does the ending become a full extra syllable, /ɪd/.
fields.next_label: Practise hearing the three ending sounds
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: We walked to the station, played cards on the train, and waited an hour for the bus.
fields.watch_out: The classic error is pronouncing the ending as an extra syllable on every verb, because the spelling suggests one. That extra syllable exists only after a /t/ or /d/ sound - everywhere else the ending is a single quick consonant glued to the verb, and inserting a vowel there instantly signals a learner accent.

title: Present perfect continuous

fields.examples_en:
She's been studying all night.
They've been waiting for over an hour.
How long have you been learning English?
fields.excerpt: An action that started in the past and is still going on now.
fields.explanation: Use the present perfect continuous when an action started in the past and is still true now. It ties the past to the present, which is exactly why a simple past will not do the job: "I worked here since 2019" tells an English speaker you have already left.
fields.next_label: Practise it: present perfect or past simple?
fields.subject: grammar
fields.target_en: I've been working here since 2019.
fields.watch_out: Many languages use a plain present tense for this idea, and translating it directly is the most common B1 mistake. If the action is still happening and you can say how long, English wants have/has been + -ing.

title: Question tags: the tune decides whether you are asking or checking

fields.examples_en:
It's a lovely day, isn't it?
You haven't seen my keys, have you?
She works in finance, doesn't she?
fields.excerpt: The same question tag can check or genuinely ask, and only the tune of the voice tells the listener which.
fields.explanation: The model sentence can be said with two different tunes, and the tune changes what the sentence does. With the voice falling on the tag, the speaker already believes the two people have met and is inviting the listener to confirm it: the tag is a small piece of politeness, not a question. With the voice rising on the tag, the speaker genuinely does not know and is asking. Both versions are written identically. In conversation, native listeners hear the difference instantly and answer accordingly: a falling tag gets a brief agreement, a rising tag gets real information. At this level, controlling the tune is what separates a speaker who sounds sure of the ground from one who seems to be checking everything.
fields.next_label: Next: why fast speech runs words together
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.target_en: You've met before, haven't you?
fields.watch_out: Most learners rise on every tag, because in many languages a rising tune is simply what a question sounds like. In English that habit has a cost: a speaker who rises on all their tags sounds permanently unsure, and a listener may feel interrogated by what were meant to be friendly remarks. The remark about the weather in the first example is not a request for information; it needs the falling tune. Practise the two tunes on the same sentence until you can choose one deliberately, then listen for which one native speakers use in small talk. It is nearly always the fall.

title: Understatement in senior meetings: how small words carry a large no

fields.examples_en:
That might be worth a second look before we commit.
I'd push back gently on the timing, if I may.
Shall we park that for now and come back to it?
fields.excerpt: In a British meeting the softer the wording, the firmer the objection; this lesson teaches you to hear a polite sentence at full strength.
fields.explanation: In British professional English the strength of an objection runs in the opposite direction to the strength of the words. The model sentence contains no negative judgement at all on the surface: it mentions uncertainty, a small shortfall and a vague earlier intention. Spoken by a senior person in a meeting, it usually means the proposal has been rejected or must be reworked. The mechanism is a shared convention: the more senior the speaker and the more serious the problem, the softer the wording becomes, because directness would embarrass everyone present. Native colleagues decode this without effort and change course at once. The skill at this level is not producing the sentences, which are short and simple, but hearing them at full strength and reading the room the way the speakers in it do.
fields.next_label: Hear it in a meeting: a junior proposal is quietly parked
fields.subject: business
fields.target_en: I'm not sure that's quite what we had in mind.
fields.watch_out: The danger is symmetrical. A learner who takes the soft wording literally hears a mild reservation, carries on with the plan, and is baffled weeks later to discover it was killed in that meeting. The same learner, wanting to sound decisive, states objections plainly and is heard as aggressive out of all proportion to the content. Treat all three examples as instructions, not opinions: the first is telling you to redo the work, the second says the timing is unacceptable, the third closes the topic. Reply by conceding, not by defending.

title: Three-part verbs that never split, and where each sits on the register scale

fields.error_en: I look forward to hear from you soon.
fields.examples_en:
However difficult the clients became, she refused to put up with being shouted at.
The sequel never lived up to the expectations the first film had created.
Years of quiet corner-cutting finally caught up with the firm's directors.
fields.excerpt: Ten three-word verbs that never separate, with a register note on where a single-word verb reads better.
fields.explanation: At advanced levels the trap is not learning these expressions but handling their grammar. Each one is built from a verb, an adverbial particle and a preposition, and the three words behave as a single unit of meaning: nothing can be inserted between them, and the object, whether noun or pronoun, always follows the complete chunk. That makes them simpler than their two-part cousins, which sometimes split, yet learners who have internalised the splitting rule keep trying to apply it here. Register is the second issue: some of these chunks sit happily in formal writing, while others would be replaced by a single-word verb in a report or an essay.

The chunk's final word is identical in form to the marker that introduces an infinitive, so learners follow it with the base form of a verb. In these three-part verbs, however, the last element is a true preposition, and a preposition can only be followed by a noun phrase or by the -ing form of a verb. The sentence above therefore needs an -ing form in place of the bare verb. The same logic runs through every row of the table: nothing may ever come between the three words, and whatever follows them - noun, pronoun or -ing form - must come after the complete chunk, never inside it.

title: Why you cannot hear where one word ends and the next begins

fields.examples_en:
Turn it off and put it away.
The old man must be about eighty.
Don't you want to go on without us?
fields.excerpt: How fluent speech runs words together, and the patterns that let you hear the joins.
fields.explanation: In writing, spaces show where words end. In speech there are none: a fluent speaker produces one continuous stream, and its syllables do not respect the boundaries of the written words. The two versions in the line above are the same three words; the second shows how the stream is re-cut, with each final consonant starting the next syllable. The table collects the four regular processes behind this: consonants migrating forward onto a vowel, glides inserted between vowels, /t/ and /d/ deleted inside consonant clusters, and sounds altered or fused by a neighbour. None of it is careless speech; it is the system, and it is why a sentence you could read easily can be impossible to cut up by ear.

Learners do this constantly, and then blame their vocabulary: the words feel unknown when in fact every one of them is familiar. The error is the assumption underneath, that speakers separate their words and that a boundary you cannot hear means a word you do not know. Fluent speech contains no gaps whatsoever. When a stretch of speech resists you, do not reach for the dictionary first; try re-cutting the stream, moving each final consonant onto the vowel after it, and the familiar words usually reappear.

title: Everyday expressions where one word is fixed and cannot be swapped

fields.error_en: She spilt coffee on my laptop, but I'm sure she didn't do it by purpose.
fields.examples_en:
Sorry, I've changed my mind - can we meet on Thursday instead?
Take your time - the film doesn't start until eight.
I'll get in touch with the landlord about the heating.
fields.excerpt: Common fixed expressions in which one word is welded in place and cannot be swapped for a synonym.
fields.explanation: At this level you already know every individual word in these expressions. What you cannot predict is which words English has chosen and welded together. Each entry in the table is a fixed combination used constantly in everyday speech: for deciding, for helping, for staying in contact, for saying whether something was deliberate or not. The meaning of the whole is usually easy to see; the danger is producing a version of it that is almost right. Treat each row as a single item of vocabulary: learn it whole, and notice which word in it could never be guessed from the meaning alone.

Each of those expressions is welded to its own preposition, and the prepositions are not interchangeable: the deliberate one keeps the small word that opens row ten, the unintentional one keeps the small word that opens row eleven. Learners mix them because both phrases answer the same question - was it intended or not? - so the pair feels like one system with a single preposition. It is not: swap the small word and you produce something every native speaker notices at once, even though the meaning survives. title: When two near-synonyms describe the same behaviour and only one is a compliment

fields.error_en: I would describe myself as pushy about deadlines and pedantic about detail.
fields.examples_en:
Her flatmates called it stingy; she called it frugal, and neither side was describing a different set of facts.
Say that a colleague is assertive and you are recommending her; say that she is pushy and you are warning against her.
An inquisitive child is a pleasure to teach, whereas a nosy one has already asked what you earn.
fields.excerpt: Pairs of near-synonyms that describe the same behaviour, where one praises and the other criticises.
fields.explanation: At this level the hard part of vocabulary is no longer meaning. The words in the table below arrive in pairs, and the two members of a pair describe the same behaviour: a dictionary will often gloss them almost identically. What separates them is the verdict each one passes on the person described. One member praises the behaviour and the other condemns it, and that opinion is smuggled in rather than stated, so it never has to be defended. A learner who chooses by definition alone will eventually pay somebody a compliment with the wrong half of a pair, and nothing in the grammar will flag it.

The first cell holds the word, the second names the neutral term it shadows and the attitude it adds to it, and the third puts the word in a sentence where that attitude is the whole point. The rows work in pairs: an odd-numbered row and the even-numbered row beneath it cover the same behaviour, the first with approval and the second with disapproval. Where a word also belongs to a particular register, the middle cell says so.

fields.watch_out: The incorrect sentence above is an interview answer, and its two adjectives are the disapproving members of the pairs in rows nine and ten and in rows five and six. The speaker intends to say that he keeps a schedule moving and that he checks his work closely, which is what the approving member of each pair would have conveyed. Both adjectives are grammatically correct, both sit inside the intended meaning, and both are longer and more emphatic than the neutral term, which is exactly why a learner reaches for them. The result is a candidate who has described himself as someone who bullies the people around him and spends his working day on what does not matter. Nothing in the structure signals the damage, so nothing prompts a correction.

title: Expressions you can half-guess: the body, the weather and money

fields.error_en: We do not see eyes to eye with the new supplier about the delivery dates.
fields.examples_en:
Since the enquiry opened, the deputy head has been under a cloud, and nobody will say how long it will last.
We would love to come, but could we take a rain check and make it the following weekend instead?
Both grants ended in June, so the department is tightening its belt and asking staff to foot the bill for conferences.
fields.excerpt: Expressions built from the body, the weather and money, half guessable from their ordinary words.
fields.explanation: Every expression in the table below is built from ordinary words: parts of the body, the weather, and the everyday talk of earning and paying. That is exactly what makes them risky. The literal words point roughly at the meaning, so a reader guesses right about half the time and then stops looking. What they never reveal is the wording, which is frozen, or the situation, which is far narrower than the guess. Some of these belong in a written report; others would sound strange anywhere except among friends. The third column exists for that reason.

Two people are involved, and each of them has two of the body part concerned, so the plural looks like ordinary agreement. title: Five written vowels, roughly twenty spoken ones: why spelling misleads

fields.examples_en:
The cat sat in the car.
I put the cup down.
There is a book about food on the shelf.
fields.excerpt: Five written vowels stand for roughly twenty spoken sounds; this chart shows which letter gives which.
fields.explanation: English uses five vowel letters, and a sixth that behaves like one when it is not doing consonant work. Spoken English uses somewhere between sixteen and twenty vowel sounds, depending on the accent. The letters were fixed by printers several centuries ago, the sounds went on changing afterwards, and thousands of words arrived from other languages with their original spellings intact. The result is that one written vowel stands for several different spoken vowels, and nothing in the letter tells you which one is meant. That is why the spelling system feels arbitrary to a beginner: it is not a code for the sounds, but a record of where each word came from.

The assumption is tempting because most learners come from a language that is spelled consistently, and expecting the same here fails on the commonest words of all.

title: Point, surface, container: one scale for both time and place

fields.error_en: The meeting is in Tuesday, and I will call you in the next week.
fields.examples_en:
The shop opens at nine on weekdays and closes in the evening.
He waited at the bus stop on the corner in the rain.
We arrived in Lisbon on the fourteenth at midnight.
fields.excerpt: Point, surface and container: one scale that chooses the preposition for both time and place.
fields.explanation: Three prepositions carry most of the work of locating something in time or in space, and they are usually taught as six separate lists to memorise. They are better understood as one scale of precision. The first treats what follows as a point with no size worth mentioning. The second treats it as a surface or a bounded stretch you sit on rather than inside. The third treats it as a container with an interior that surrounds you. That ordering governs clock times and countries alike, which is why the model sentence above can run through all three in a row without changing its logic.
fields.subject: grammar
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Kind</th><th scope="col">Level</th><th scope="col">Used for</th><th scope="col">Example</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Read each row across. The first column says whether the row is about time or place, the second gives the level on the scale, the third what kinds of word belong there, and the fourth an example. The second half adds a preposition to an expression that already refuses one: anything opening with the words for this, last, next or every stands alone, and inserting a preposition in front is the single most frequent error with these three words. title: Which word goes in front of the noun, and when nothing does

fields.error_en: She gave me an advice about the interview, so I bought new suit.
fields.examples_en:
I need a chair for the meeting, and the chair in the corner will do.
Cats sleep for most of the day, but the cats next door never seem to.
She studies medicine at university in a city I have never visited.
fields.excerpt: The indefinite article, the definite article and no article at all, with the meaning each choice carries.
fields.explanation: English offers three articles-worth of choice in front of a noun, not two, because using nothing at all is itself a grammatical option with its own meaning. The indefinite article introduces one item the listener has not met before and is singular only. The definite article claims the listener can work out which one you mean, and works with singular, plural and uncountable nouns alike. No article at all makes a general statement, and is available only to plural and uncountable nouns. A singular countable noun therefore always needs one of the two articles or another determiner: it is the one case where leaving the slot empty is never correct.

Learners whose first language has no articles produce the second error constantly and rarely notice it, because nothing about the sentence sounds broken to them. I live with my family in a small town, and I study English twice a week.

Both are in their present form, while the time word at the front has already placed everything in a finished day, so the sentence contradicts itself. This happens because the three pictures are in front of you as you write, which makes the events feel present, and because present forms are what an A2 candidate produces fastest under time pressure. title: Choosing the right line for each move in a work email

I am writing to confirm the details of Thursday's meeting.
Could you let me know by Wednesday whether the room is still free?
Thank you for your help - I look forward to hearing from you.
fields.excerpt: A work email is a sequence of moves; here is a ready-made line for each move at three levels of formality.
fields.explanation: A work email is not a piece of continuous writing. It is a short sequence of moves: you say what has prompted the message, you ask for something, you press for an answer when nothing comes back, you acknowledge a late response, and you close. Each move has a small stock of ready-made wordings that people reuse almost unchanged, so they are worth learning whole rather than assembled from scratch. Choosing between two wordings for the same move is rarely a question of meaning. The pair at the top of this page makes the same opening move twice, once at a formal distance and once as one colleague to another.

fields.watch_out: Three things go wrong in the incorrect sentence above, and each of them is tempting. The verb it opens with needs a preposition before its object in English, while its nearest equivalent in several other languages takes an object directly, so the small word is simply left out. The time word before the day marks the end of a continuous stretch, which suggests you will sit at your desk all week; a deadline needs the other preposition, the one meaning at some point before. And the formula of gratitude at the end, offered before the reader has agreed to anything, quietly removes their right to refuse. Keep it for after they have acted, or use it only for something they have already promised.

title: Which syllable carries the beat, and what makes it move

fields.error_en: The council would not PERmit us to start, so we lost the conTRACT.
fields.examples_en:
We could not get a permit, and the council will not permit the work.
Sales showed a small increase, and prices will increase again in June.
The economic situation made their decision harder than anyone expected.
fields.excerpt: Which syllable carries the beat in longer words, and the endings that make the beat move.
fields.explanation: Every English word of more than one syllable has exactly one main beat. The syllable carrying it is longer, louder and slightly higher in pitch, while the others shrink and their vowels tend to collapse into the neutral central sound English uses wherever there is no stress. Putting the beat in the wrong place therefore damages you more than mispronouncing a consonant: listeners recognise a word by its rhythm before they have finished hearing its vowels. Two forces decide where it sits. One is the word's grammatical class, which separates the two members of each pair in the upper half of the table. The other is the ending, because certain suffixes fix the beat at a set distance from the end.

title: Words for what you eat: which take a plural and which never do

fields.error_en: I ate two breads and some rices for the lunch.
fields.examples_en:
There is some bread on the table, and there are two eggs in the pan.
How much rice do you want, and how many potatoes shall I cook?
We ordered three coffees after dinner and shared a plate of cheese.
fields.excerpt: Food words sorted into the ones that take a plural and the ones that never do, with the quantity words each accepts.
fields.explanation: Every noun in this area belongs to one of two grammatical classes, and the class decides what may stand in front of it. Countable nouns name separate objects: they accept a number, the indefinite article and a plural ending, and a question about quantity uses the plural quantifier. Uncountable nouns name a substance or a category seen as one mass: they take no number, no indefinite article and no plural ending, and quantity is expressed with the mass quantifier or with a unit word joined by a preposition. A few nouns sit in both classes and change meaning as they cross.

The first two nouns name substances rather than objects, so English treats each as a single mass: no number may stand in front of them and no plural ending may be added, and a quantity has to be supplied by a unit word with a linking preposition. Learners add the ending because their own language counts these things happily. The second mistake is the article in front of the last noun. The three daily events are used bare when you mean the event itself, and the definite article appears only when you are pointing at one particular occasion both speakers already have in mind.

title: Naming the people you are related to, by blood and by marriage

fields.error_en: The sister of my father is my aunt, and my two brother-in-laws live nearby.
fields.examples_en:
My mother's brother is my uncle, and his daughter is my cousin.
I get on well with both of my brothers-in-law and with my mother-in-law.
After my father remarried I gained a stepmother and, two years later, a half-sister.
fields.excerpt: Family words in three layers: the household, the wider family, and relatives by marriage.
fields.explanation: English names family connections in three layers, and each layer is built differently. The first covers the household you grow up in: a separate noun for each position, marked for sex, with a collective plural for the pair who raise you. The second reaches sideways, to the generation above you and to the children of that generation; one sex-marked pair covers the older line whichever side of the family it sits on, and a single common-gender noun covers the younger. The third layer is not inherited but acquired: marriage attaches a fixed tail to a word you already know, while a remarriage in the household attaches a short prefix to the front of another.

title: Openings and farewells, from the most formal to the most relaxed

fields.excerpt: Greetings and goodbyes arranged from the most formal to the most relaxed, with the situation each one suits.
fields.explanation: English has no separate polite and familiar pronouns, so much of the weight of respect and distance falls on the phrase you open with. That first phrase tells the other person how close you believe the two of you already are. A long opening with a title and a surname, like the one in the top row, sets a respectful distance; the clipped one-word form further down closes that distance to almost nothing. Neither is more correct than the other. What matters is that the distance you claim matches the distance the other person expects, because a mismatch is heard instantly, long before anyone notices your grammar.

title: Writing the numbers from 1 to 100 in words, with the usual spelling traps

fields.error_en: My brother is twenty one and my mother is fivety three.
fields.examples_en:
There are twenty-eight students in the class and only fifteen chairs.
My sister is thirteen and my mother is thirty-nine.
The tickets cost forty-five pounds each, and the hall holds ninety-nine people.
fields.excerpt: Every number from 1 to 100 written out, with the spelling traps in the teens, the tens and the hyphenated forms.
fields.explanation: The words for 1 to 12 are separate items and have to be learnt one by one, because nothing in them can be worked out. From 13 to 19 each word is built on the unit, sometimes slightly reshaped, plus one fixed ending; the multiples of 10 are built on those same stems with a different ending, which is why the two series are so easily confused in writing and in speech. Everything from 21 to 99 is then assembled from those sets: the multiple of 10 first, the unit second, joined by a hyphen. The round figure at the top of the range needs a determiner in front of it and stays singular. These are the cardinal numbers, used for counting; the ordinals used for ranking form a separate series.

title: The letters that are spelled but never spoken

fields.error_en: I don't now what to do, so please rite it down for me.
fields.examples_en:
I know the answer, but I can't write it very well.
We waited an hour outside the castle.
Please keep the receipt - the shop closes at half past five on Wednesday.
fields.excerpt: The letters that are written but never spoken, grouped into the small number of patterns they follow.
fields.explanation: Many common English words keep a letter that stopped being pronounced centuries ago. These letters are not scattered at random: they cluster into a small number of patterns, so once you know the pattern you can predict dozens of other words. The spelling never changes to match the sound, so the letter still has to be written. The only real fix is to hear each word correctly and store that sound next to the spelling.

title: Two-part verbs and their single-word formal twins

fields.error_en: Sorry, I can't come tonight - I need to ascertain what my flatmate is doing first.
fields.examples_en:
He acknowledged the delay in his statement and never once owned up to causing it.
The board agreed to postpone the vote, having quietly backed down the week before.
Every serious plan for the site has come up against the same objection from the parish council.
fields.excerpt: Two-part verbs paired with the single Latin-origin word that replaces each one in formal writing.
fields.explanation: English usually offers two ways to name the same action: a short verb followed by a small particle, and a single word of Latin origin. At lower levels the pair looks like a simple choice between casual and formal, and for the commonest rows that is all it is. Higher up, the second column stops being a neutral synonym. The formal member can admit a fact while quietly leaving the fault unadmitted, or turn a routine check into an official proceeding, or read as an accusation where the everyday form only described what happened.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Phrasal verb</th><th scope="col">Formal equivalent</th><th scope="col">What changes with the formal word</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Read each row across. The first column gives the everyday two-part verb, the second the single formal word usually offered as its equivalent, and the third says what changes when you move from one to the other - not only how formal it sounds, but what it implies about fault, permanence, method, or the speaker's power to decide. The third column is the real content here; the first two are only the pair it hangs on.
fields.table_rows: put offpostponeThe formal word states that a new date is intended; the everyday form can leak reluctance, and often does. look intoinvestigateThe formal word turns a routine check into a proceeding with a file and a finding, and quietly makes someone a suspect. find outascertainThe formal word claims the fact was established by proper procedure rather than simply discovered; it belongs to legal and official writing. put up withtolerateThe formal word is colder about people and implies the speaker had the standing to refuse and chose not to. set upestablishThe formal word confers permanence and legitimacy; the everyday form leaves the thing sounding provisional. carry outconductThe formal word implies method and design, which is why research and interviews take it; the everyday form suits instructions handed down. get rid ofeliminateThe formal word is total and technical, and applied to people it reads as a euphemism rather than a softening. play downminimiseThe formal word is what an inquiry writes when it is assigning blame; the everyday form reports the same behaviour more lightly. do away withabolishThe formal word belongs to law and institutions and treats the thing as an established right or rule; the everyday form can sound flippant about something serious. back downconcedeThe formal word allows a reasoned yielding and leaves the dignity intact; the everyday form implies a loss of face under pressure. own up toacknowledgeThe formal word admits the fact and leaves the fault open; the everyday form admits the fault outright, which is why it costs something to say. come up againstencounterThe formal word is neutral and clinical; the everyday form builds in the resistance, the sense of something pushing back.

fields.watch_out: The two columns are not a swap list, and at this level the third column is the whole point. A second-column word dropped into conversation with friends sounds pompous or faintly sarcastic, and a first-column form dropped into a formal report reads as careless. The real danger is rows two, eight and eleven, where the formal member does not merely raise the register: it accuses, or it quietly withdraws an admission you thought you were making. Before you choose, ask what the word does to the person it describes, not which of the two looks harder.

title: Shortening a clause down to its verb form

fields.error_en: Having reviewed your application carefully, a place on the course has been offered to you.
fields.examples_en:
Having read the file twice, I still could not see where the money had gone.
Left to itself, the argument would have burned out within a week.
Walking back from the station, I realised I had left my laptop on the train.
fields.excerpt: How a full clause shortens to its verb form, what the shortened clause can and cannot do, and the classic error.
fields.explanation: A participle clause is an ordinary clause with its subject and its finite verb stripped out, leaving only the verb form. What remains has no subject of its own, so it silently borrows one from the main clause, and that borrowed subject is the whole trick of the structure. The form you choose encodes the relationship: one form for an action running at the same time or supplying the cause, another for an action completed before the main one, and another when the shortened half is passive. This is a compression device, at home in writing far more than in speech.
fields.subject: grammar
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Full clause</th><th scope="col">Reduced clause</th><th scope="col">Relationship encoded</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Read each row across. The first column is the full clause with every part present, the second is the same idea shortened to a verb form, and the third names the relationship that particular form encodes - same time, cause, earlier action, condition or passive. In every row without exception, the person or thing performing the shortened action is the subject of the main clause.
