fields.target_en: Because she felt unwell, she left - Feeling unwell, she left
fields.watch_out: Everything here depends on the subject. The shortened half takes the subject of the main clause whether you meant it to or not, so the moment the doer changes between the two halves, the sentence quietly claims something absurd. Check rows four and five as well: the form used there places its action before the main verb, so substituting the same-time form loses the sequence you were trying to show. And keep to two or three reduced clauses in a paragraph at most - past that the prose loses its joints and every sentence starts to sound like a committee report.

title: Turning actions into nouns to lift the register

fields.error_en: The failing of the pilot scheme was caused by the refusing of the council to fund it.
fields.examples_en:
Analysis of the transcripts suggests that the interviewer shaped most of the answers.
The failure of the scheme owed less to funding than to the assumption that families would move.
Any reduction in tuition fees would have to be matched by an increase in public funding.
fields.excerpt: Turning verbs into nouns to lift the register of an essay, with the endings that build each noun.
fields.explanation: Nominalisation turns an action word into a thing word, so that the action itself can become the subject or object of the sentence. This does two jobs at once in an exam essay: it packs more information into fewer clauses, and it lifts the register, because formal written English prefers to discuss processes rather than people doing things. The noun is rarely predictable from the action word, so each pair has to be learned as a pair. The cost is that the doer disappears from view.
fields.subject: exams
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Verb</th><th scope="col">Noun form</th><th scope="col">The noun in a sentence</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: The first column is the action word, the second is the noun built from it, and the third shows that noun carrying the weight of a sentence. The third column is where the register actually changes: the noun has become the subject or the object, and the sentence no longer needs to name who acted. Read down the second column and note how unpredictable the endings are.
fields.table_rows: decidedecisionThe committee's decision came as a surprise to everyone. growgrowthGrowth in the sector has slowed for three consecutive quarters. failfailureThe failure of the pilot scheme was entirely predictable. analyseanalysisAnalysis of the survey data reveals two distinct groups. reducereductionA reduction in class size improves outcomes only up to a point. expandexpansionExpansion into overseas markets carries obvious risks. arrivearrivalThe arrival of cheap solar panels changed the calculation entirely. argueargumentThe argument for a second vote rests on a single point. refuserefusalHer refusal to comment was widely reported. assumeassumptionThis assumption is never tested anywhere in the paper. respondresponseThe government's response to the report was slow and defensive. applyapplicationApplication of the rule to part-time staff remains unclear.
fields.target_en: decide - decision / analyse - analysis / refuse - refusal
fields.watch_out: There are two traps. The first is the form itself: the endings are not predictable, and guessing produces something no examiner will read as academic writing. Rows two, three, seven, eight, nine and eleven each take a different ending from the commonest one, and row four rebuilds the word instead of adding anything to it - those seven have to be learned one at a time. The second trap is greed. Examiners penalise essays built entirely from abstract nouns, because such writing stops saying who did what and becomes impossible to argue with. Use the pattern to carry your topic sentences, and let ordinary action words do the work in between.

title: Which strong adverb goes with which adjective

fields.error_en: We are highly grateful for your help and hugely concerned about the delay.
fields.examples_en:
She was bitterly disappointed, though she was fully aware that the decision had been coming for months.
It is highly unlikely that the committee will meet before September.
We are deeply grateful for everything you did that week.
fields.excerpt: Strong adverbs keep a small circle of regular adjective partners; this table lists the pairs worth learning.
fields.explanation: Strong adverbs in English do not attach freely to any adjective; each one keeps a small circle of regular partners, and the pairing is remembered as a unit rather than worked out from meaning. Choosing the partner a fluent speaker expects is one of the clearest signals that you control the language rather than translate into it. The all-purpose intensifier everyone learns first is not wrong, but it flattens every statement to the same level and tells the reader nothing. Swapping an adverb from one row into another usually produces a sentence that breaks no rule and is completely dead on the page.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Adverb</th><th scope="col">Adjectives it pairs with</th><th scope="col">Example</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: The first column is the strong adverb, the second lists the adjectives it habitually goes with, and the third shows one of those pairs at work in a full sentence. Learn each row as a single block rather than as an adverb plus a choice. The second column is not a complete list, but anything outside it is worth checking before you use it.
fields.table_rows: bitterlydisappointed, cold, dividedShe was bitterly disappointed by the decision. utterlyconvinced, exhausted, ridiculousHe seemed utterly convinced that the figures were wrong. highlyunlikely, recommended, controversialIt is highly unlikely that the flight will leave tonight. deeplyconcerned, grateful, offendedThe board is deeply concerned about the delay. painfullyaware, obvious, slowHe was painfully aware that everyone was waiting for him. widelyregarded, believed, availableShe is widely regarded as the best in the field. fullyaware, booked, refundableWe are fully aware of the risks. perfectlyclear, reasonable, happyLet me make one thing perfectly clear. hugelysuccessful, popular, influentialThe campaign was hugely successful in the north. seriouslyinjured, ill, understaffedNobody was seriously injured in the crash.
fields.target_en: bitterly disappointed - highly unlikely - deeply grateful
fields.watch_out: These pairs are learned, not reasoned out. Two adverbs in the table sit beside the same adjective, in rows five and seven, and they do not mean the same thing: one adds discomfort about what is known, the other only completeness of knowledge. Rows one and four also look interchangeable and are not - the first carries resentment, the second carries gravity and concern. Finally, resist the urge to intensify everything: three strong pairs in a paragraph is already a lot, and the fourth simply stops being heard.

title: Set expressions for saying something was easy or hard

fields.error_en: Don't worry about the interview - it's a piece of pie.
fields.examples_en:
The exam itself was a piece of cake; getting to the hall on time was not.
Persuading the finance team to release the money was like pulling teeth.
Turning the whole site round before Christmas is a tall order, but it is not impossible.
fields.excerpt: Ready-made expressions for saying that something was effortless or a struggle, sorted by tone.
fields.explanation: English keeps a large stock of ready-made expressions for saying that something was effortless or that it was a grind, and speakers reach for them constantly. Each one is frozen: the words are fixed, and the whole expression behaves as a single description after the verb of being. What separates them is not meaning but register and setting - some are perfectly safe in a report, others belong only to conversation between people who know each other. The third column is therefore the one that matters most at this level.

fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Expression</th><th scope="col">Meaning</th><th scope="col">Typical use and register</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: The first column gives the expression exactly as it is said, the second gives its meaning in ordinary words, and the third tells you where it belongs: whether you could write it in a work email or should keep it for speech, and how strong it sounds. The first six rows describe things that were easy; the last six describe things that were hard.
fields.table_rows: a piece of cakeVery easy indeedSpeech and informal writing; the most common of all, and a little worn. a walk in the parkEasy and untroublingSpeech; very often used in the negative to say the opposite. child's playEasy for anyone with the skillSpeech and journalism; can sound dismissive of the task or the person. plain sailingSmooth and free of problems, usually after a difficult startSpeech and neutral writing; safe in a work email. a breezeEffortlessSpeech only, informal; more common in American English. no trouble at allEasily done, and done gladlySpeech; a polite reply when someone thanks you or apologises for asking. a hard nut to crackA problem or a person that resists every approachSpeech and journalism; used of people as well as problems. an uphill battleA long effort against strong resistanceSpeech and writing; safe in reports and news. no picnicUnpleasant and hard goingSpeech, informal; understatement, usually about something you survived. easier said than doneSimple to suggest, hard to carry outSpeech and writing; a mild objection to someone else's advice. like pulling teethPainfully slow because the other side will not cooperateSpeech, informal; about extracting information or agreement from someone. a tall orderA demand that is very hard to meetSpeech and writing; safe in business, often about deadlines or targets.

fields.watch_out: These are stored whole, not assembled from parts. Swapping in a word that means much the same thing kills the expression outright: the nouns in rows one, two and nine are locked, and a perfectly reasonable synonym in their place produces something no speaker has ever said. Read the third column as carefully as the second - rows five, nine and eleven belong to speech among people you know, and dropping one into a message to a client reads as sloppy rather than warm. Finally, row two is most often heard in the negative, which flips it into the opposite of the meaning listed beside it.

I'm tired, but the kids are ready to go.
She's a nurse at the hospital in town.
We aren't late - the bus is early.

fields.explanation: English speakers use this verb to say who they are, how they feel, and where things are - no other verb appears more often. title: The busiest verb and its two-part combinations

I'll get back to you as soon as I hear anything.
She never really got over losing that job.
How do you get by without a car out here?

Both of my children have brown eyes.
How many people are coming tonight?
He lost two teeth playing hockey.

These are very old forms that survived because the words are so common - you meet them every day, so there is no way around memorising them. fields.error_en: Your going to love it here.

It's been years since the band changed its sound.
They're convinced their flight leaves from there.
Who's going to tell her whose fault it really was?

The reliable test is substitution: expand the apostrophe form into its full two words and see whether the sentence still works; if it does not, you needed the possessive spelling. Spell-checkers miss most of these, because every wrong choice is still a real word.

title: What comes after the verb: the two patterns

fields.error_en: I enjoy to travel with my family.
fields.examples_en:
I really enjoy working from home two days a week.
She decided to apply for the job in the end.
Please remember to send the report before five.
fields.excerpt: Which verbs are followed by the -ing form and which by the to-form, learned pair by pair.
fields.explanation: Some verbs must be followed by the -ing form, others by the to-form, and the choice is fixed by the first verb, not by meaning - you simply learn each verb together with its pattern. A third, smaller group accepts both forms with a change of meaning, and the last three rows of the table belong to it. In rows 9 and 10 the -ing form looks back at something real - an activity in progress or a past event - while the to-form looks ahead to a purpose or a duty; in row 11 the -ing form proposes an experiment to see what happens, while the to-form reports an effort that may or may not succeed.

fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Verb</th><th scope="col">Followed by</th><th scope="col">Example</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: The middle column tells you which form follows the verb. The last three rows take both forms, and their example column shows the two meanings side by side.

fields.watch_out: When both forms are possible (the last three rows), do not treat them as interchangeable: in row 9 the -ing form means quitting an activity while the to-form means pausing in order to do it, and in row 10 the -ing form recalls a past event while the to-form is about a duty not to forget. Picking the wrong one produces a grammatical sentence that says something you did not mean - which is much harder to notice than an ordinary mistake.

title: Connectors that hold an essay together

fields.error_en: The plan is popular, however it will be expensive.
fields.examples_en:
The scheme is expensive. However, it has clear long-term benefits.
Although the sample was small, the results were consistent.
In conclusion, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.
fields.excerpt: The connectors that make an essay's logic visible, grouped by the relationship each one signals.
fields.explanation: Examiners reward essays whose logic is visible, and these words are the signposts that make it visible - each one announces the relationship between what you just said and what comes next. The table groups them by the job they do; within a group the members are close in meaning but differ in position and punctuation, which is where most marks are lost. Two or three per group, used accurately, beat a dozen used at random.

fields.table_intro: First column: the logical job the word does. Third column: where the word sits and the punctuation it needs - learn position and punctuation together with the word itself.

And resist decorating every sentence with a signpost: use one only where the logical link would otherwise be unclear.

title: Ready-made lines for opening and closing an email

fields.error_en: Dear Mr Evans, give me a shout when the report is ready.
fields.examples_en:
Dear Ms Carter, I am writing with regard to the March invoice.
I've attached the report - could you get back to me by Friday?
Please do not hesitate to contact me if you have any questions.
fields.excerpt: Opening and closing lines for workplace email, sorted by how formal the relationship is.
fields.explanation: Readers of workplace email judge the tone before they read the content, and the opening and closing lines carry most of that tone. The table sorts ready-made lines into three levels of formality; the safe rule is to pick one column and stay in it from the first line to the last. The middle column is the default for most everyday work email - keep the first for strangers, officials and first contact, and the last for colleagues you already chat with.

fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Purpose</th><th scope="col">Formal</th><th scope="col">Neutral</th><th scope="col">Informal</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Each row is one job a line does in an email. The three columns give that line at three levels of formality, from most formal on the left to most relaxed on the right.

fields.watch_out: Never mix columns: a formal greeting followed by a chatty closing line reads as careless, not friendly. Note the pairing rule in the last two rows - the formal sign-off in row 9 goes with a greeting that names the person, while the one in row 10 belongs with the nameless greeting in row 2. Greetings and sign-offs end with a comma, never a full stop.

title: The small words that follow common adjectives

fields.error_en: She is married with an engineer.
fields.examples_en:
I've always been interested in old maps.
She's really good at making people feel welcome.
He's responsible for the whole booking system.
fields.excerpt: Common adjectives with the fixed small word that follows each one.
fields.explanation: Certain adjectives come with a fixed small word after them, and the pair works as a single unit - the small word carries no meaning of its own and cannot be worked out from logic or from your own language. Learn the pair together, as one vocabulary item, the way you would learn a new word. When a verb follows the pair, it takes the -ing form, never the to-form.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Adjective</th><th scope="col">Preposition</th><th scope="col">Example</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Middle column: the fixed small word that belongs to the adjective in the first column. The example shows the pair working as one unit inside a sentence.
fields.table_rows: afraidofHe's afraid of flying. goodatShe's good at explaining things. badatI'm bad at remembering names. interestedinAre you interested in photography? responsibleforWho is responsible for the schedule? proudofWe're proud of what the team built. marriedtoShe's married to a doctor. famousforThe town is famous for its cheese. worriedaboutI'm worried about the exam. differentfromThe film is very different from the book.
fields.target_en: interested in - good at - afraid of
fields.watch_out: Do not translate the small word from your own language - the English choice rarely matches, and row 7 is the classic trap because most languages use their word for accompaniment there, while English uses a direction word instead. Whenever you learn a new adjective, write down its partner word at the same time; guessing later almost always fails.

title: The irregular past forms you cannot avoid

fields.error_en: I have saw that film.
fields.examples_en:
She has gone home already.
I saw that film last week.
Have you written the email yet?
fields.excerpt: The ten irregular past forms you will meet every single day, with both past forms side by side.
fields.explanation: English has about 200 verbs that refuse the -ed rule, and a handful of them do most of the work in real conversation. This table gives you the ten you will meet every single day. Learn the three forms as one unit, out loud, in order - the rhythm is what sticks.

fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Base form</th><th scope="col">Past simple</th><th scope="col">Past participle</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Three columns: the base form you find in a dictionary, the past simple you use for finished time, and the past participle you use after have, has and had.
fields.table_rows: gowentgoneseesawseentaketooktakencomecamecomegetgotgotmakemademadeknowknewknownthinkthoughtthoughtgivegavegivenwritewrotewritten
fields.target_en: go - went - gone
fields.watch_out: The most common mistake at this level is using the past simple after have. The second and third columns look interchangeable but never are: the middle column stands alone, the right column always needs have, has or had in front of it.

title: Learned words whose spelling hides the way they are said

fields.error_en: hyperbole - HY-per-bowl
fields.examples_en:
Calling it the worst day in the company's history was pure hyperbole.
The plan went awry within a week of the launch.
The choir rehearses on the quay every Thursday evening.
fields.excerpt: Ten educated words, most of them from Greek and French, that kept spellings the ordinary rules cannot read, each with a plain respelling.
fields.explanation: Advanced readers meet these words on the page long before they hear them, and the page misleads. Most of them arrived from Greek or French and kept a spelling that the ordinary rules of English cannot read: a final letter that is a full syllable, a vowel letter that is silent, a consonant spoken as a different one, a stress that sits one syllable later than the eye expects. Because the words belong to educated speech, a wrong reading is noticed and remembered. The table gives each word once, with a plain respelling in which capital letters mark the stressed syllable, and a note on the trap the spelling sets.

The cure is not a rule but a list: these words are few, they are learned one by one, and the safest habit is to say a new learned word aloud once, from a dictionary, before ever using it in a meeting or a presentation.

title: British place names that are not said the way they are written

fields.error_en: Leicester - LIE-ches-ter
fields.examples_en:
The train to Leicester leaves from platform four.
She grew up in Norwich and moved to Greenwich for work.
Our head office is in Reading, not in Derby.
fields.excerpt: Ten British place names whose spelling is centuries out of date, with the local pronunciation and the three patterns that explain most of them.
fields.explanation: British place names are the last place where the spelling of the Middle Ages survives untouched while the pronunciation has moved on for six centuries. Whole syllables have been swallowed, and the spelling never caught up. A fluent speaker who reads one of these names as written is marked at once as a stranger, and in a business or travel setting that is worth avoiding. The names in the table are the ones you will actually need: large cities, transport hubs and London districts. Each comes with a plain respelling, stressed syllable in capitals, and a note on the pattern it belongs to, because most of these names follow one of three habits and knowing the habit lets you guess the rest.

fields.table_head: <tr><th scope="col">Place</th><th scope="col">Sounds like</th><th scope="col">Pattern</th></tr>
fields.table_intro: Read each row as the name, the way local speakers say it, and the pattern it follows. Three patterns cover most of the table: an internal syllable that has been swallowed, a written ending that has shrunk to a single weak sound, and a spelling that matches an older pronunciation or a different word altogether.

fields.watch_out: The error above reads the name in row one letter by letter, producing three syllables where local speech has two. It is the single most recognisable outsider's mistake in British English, and the names in rows two and three invite exactly the same one. The safest habit is to trust the pattern column: once you know that this family of names swallows its middle syllable, you will read a new name of the same shape correctly the first time. When in doubt, listen for the announcement on the platform before you say the name yourself.

title: Find the word that takes the beat when a sentence corrects an idea

fields.answer_note: In every item the first half of the sentence names an idea and the second half replaces it, and the replacement is always the missing word. That is the word a fluent speaker hits hardest, because stress follows information, not position: whatever is new or contrasting takes the beat, and everything already known steps back. The typical error at this level is mechanical placement - learners land the stress on the last word or on the negative, no matter where the real contrast sits. Look at the fourth item: the missing word falls in the middle of the line, not at the end, yet it takes the strongest beat. The logic that found each answer is the logic the ear needs in listening: identify what is being corrected, and the beat locates itself.
fields.excerpt: Find the word that carries the strongest beat when a sentence rejects one idea and replaces it with another.
fields.focus_en:
I didn't order the soup - I ordered the salad.
The film wasn't boring; it was brilliant.
fields.instruction: Each sentence rejects one idea and replaces it with another. The replacement - the new information - is the word that would carry the strongest beat, and it is the word that is missing. Use the meaning of the surrounding sentence to supply it, one word per gap. Then read the whole line aloud: give your word the full beat, and let the grammar words around it shrink to almost nothing.
fields.items_en:
1. I didn't say he stole the money - he only ___ it, and he gave it back a week later.
2. The bag isn't heavy at all - in fact it's surprisingly ___.
3. He isn't my friend - he's my ___: we grew up in the same house, with the same parents.
4. She didn't fail her driving test - she ___ it at the first attempt.
5. I ordered one ticket, but the machine printed ___, so I gave the spare one to a colleague.
fields.subject: pronunciation

title: Restore the unguessable word in each everyday expression

fields.answer_note: Every answer is a noun, and in each case it is the one word the expression froze long ago. The classic errors: in item three, learners offer the ordinary noun for assistance, which no native speaker uses in this frame; in item five, many reach for a noun meaning the faculty of remembering, because that is what their own language fixes there - though a few languages happen to fix the very organ English chose, so check rather than translate. In items one, two and four the temptation is a more logical noun: one meaning decision, one meaning a look, one meaning contact. Resist all of them. The test: if a synonym still sounds acceptable in the gap, you have not yet learned the expression as one frozen unit.
fields.excerpt: Restore the one unpredictable word in each fixed everyday expression.
fields.focus_en:
You don't have to decide today - take your time.
Come round whenever suits you - it's up to you.
fields.instruction: Each sentence below is missing one word. The gap always hides the frozen part of a fixed everyday expression - the word you could not predict from the meaning alone. Write a single word in each gap; no other word, however logical it seems, will be accepted.
fields.items_en:
1. I can't make up my ___ - the blue jacket or the green one?
2. Could you keep an ___ on my suitcase while I buy the tickets?
3. This box is really heavy - could you give me a ___?
4. We promised to keep in ___ after the course finished, and we still write every month.
5. Our teacher wants us to learn the whole dialogue by ___ for Monday.
fields.subject: idioms

title: The half you cannot guess: expressions about the body, weather and money

fields.answer_note: In every item the gap falls on the word that carries none of the meaning, because that is the word a learner cannot reconstruct. Item one is the clearest case: the ordinary verb for settling an account fits the sense perfectly and is what most people write, yet the fixed version uses a quite different verb, one with no connection to paying at all. In item two the noun stays bare and plural, with no article and no possessive, and a singular form is the usual slip. Item three fixes the container, and the American version of the same expression uses a different one, so learners who have met that variety supply it with confidence. Items four and five gap the half that is frozen rather than the half that hints at the sense.
fields.excerpt: Fill the gap that hides the fixed word in expressions about the body, the weather and money.
fields.focus_en:
Could you give me a hand with these boxes, and keep an eye on the door while I am upstairs?
The venue cost an arm and a leg, and two of the organisers got cold feet a week before the conference.
fields.instruction: Each sentence below is missing one word from a fixed expression. In every case the gap falls on the word you could not have worked out from the meaning, while the words that are easy to supply have been left in place. Write the missing word only, in the form the sentence requires. If an ordinary alternative seems to fit the sense perfectly, treat that as a warning rather than an encouragement: it is almost certainly not the answer.
fields.items_en:
1. The organisers will ___ the bill for travel, so you only need to pay for your own meals.
2. Her wages barely cover the rent, and she has been struggling to make ___ meet since April.
3. Nobody was hurt and the repair took an hour, but the local paper turned it into a storm in a ___.
4. I cannot manage Thursday, but could I take a ___ check and come the week after instead?
5. With both grants gone, the whole team had to ___ their belts for the rest of the year.
fields.subject: idioms

title: The word changes if you drop the last sound: complete each sentence

fields.answer_note: In every pair the two words share the same opening and the same vowel, so only the last sound separates them. A learner who lets that sound fade produces the shorter member of the pair every time, and the listener has nothing else in the word to work with. The first three pairs are ordinary vocabulary, so a lost ending simply delivers a different word and a puzzled face. The last two are more serious, because the sound that goes missing is the whole of the grammar: in the fourth item it is the only mark of a present verb with a third-person subject, and in the fifth it is the only thing placing the action in the past, which the time expression closing that line has already fixed.
fields.excerpt: Two words that differ only in their final sound: say both and choose the one the sentence needs.
fields.focus_en:
My brother helps in the kitchen and he cooked dinner last night.
We need two more chairs for our guests.
fields.instruction: Each sentence below has a gap, and two possible words are printed in brackets at the end of the line. The two are identical except for the sound at the very end. Say both of them aloud at normal speed and make sure you can hear a difference between them. Then decide which one the sentence actually needs, and write that word in the gap. If the two members of a pair sound the same when you say them, the ending is not being pronounced.
fields.items_en:
1. I paid for the tickets with my ___. (car / card)
2. The ___ blew all the papers off the table. (win / wind)
3. There was one empty ___ at the back of the bus. (sea / seat)
4. My sister ___ in a hospital in the city centre. (work / works)
5. We ___ tennis in the park last Sunday. (play / played)
fields.subject: pronunciation

title: Choose the word that places the sentence in time or in space

fields.answer_note: Items 1, 2 and 3 run straight up the scale: a clock time is a point, a date is a bounded surface, and a country is a container. Item 4 is the trap, and it is the commonest error with these three words: the expression already begins with a word meaning the one after this, and that whole group stands without any preposition in front. Item 5 tests whether you are reading the geometry rather than the noun, since the sentence names two pieces of furniture and only the first is the surface the umbrella is resting on; the second sits inside a container preposition of its own, which is there to distract you.
fields.excerpt: Choose the preposition that places each sentence in time or in space, or decide that none is needed.
fields.focus_en:
The train leaves at 7.30 on Tuesday.
She lives in Portugal, at an address I have forgotten.
fields.instruction: Each sentence has a gap where a word placing something in time or in space belongs. Write the one word that fits. In one of the five the correct answer is that no word belongs there at all: for that item write the word for an absence, so a deliberate choice can be told apart from a forgotten one. Ask yourself whether the thing after the gap is being treated as a point, as a surface, or as a container.
fields.items_en:
1. The meeting starts ___ nine on Thursday morning.
2. My birthday falls ___ the fourteenth of March.
3. She has lived ___ Portugal since she was a child.
4. We are going to visit them ___ next summer.
5. He left his umbrella ___ the table in the hall.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Put in the missing word, or leave the gap empty

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 2 are the same noun twice and show the core contrast: first mention, new to the reader, takes the indefinite article; second mention, made identifiable by the words following it, takes the definite one. Item 3 is a general statement about a plural noun, so nothing goes in front. Item 4 looks like item 1 but the noun is uncountable in English, which rules the indefinite article out entirely; the words after the noun make it identifiable, so the definite article is correct. Item 5 belongs to the small closed set of meals and institutions that drop the article when you mean the ordinary activity rather than a particular instance of it.
fields.excerpt: Put the right article in front of each noun, or recognise the cases where nothing belongs there.
fields.focus_en:
I saw a dog in the park. The dog was limping.
Cats sleep for most of the day.
fields.instruction: Each sentence has a gap in front of a noun. Write the one word that belongs there. In two of the five, the correct answer is that nothing belongs there at all: for those, write the word for an absence of quantity rather than leaving your answer blank, so that you can tell a deliberate choice from a forgotten one. Look at whether the noun is singular, plural or uncountable, and at whether your reader can already tell which one you mean.
fields.items_en:
1. I need ___ new chair for my office.
2. ___ chair you ordered last week has arrived.
3. ___ chairs are cheaper online than in the shops.
4. She gave me ___ advice that I still follow.
5. We had ___ breakfast before we left the house.
fields.subject: grammar

title: One sound apart: choosing the word the sentence needs

fields.answer_note: The first three answers are voiceless: the vocal cords stay still, and a listener should hear nothing but air escaping between tongue and teeth. The last two are voiced, and a finger on the throat will feel it buzz. Each answer has a near-twin one consonant away. The twin of the first names a metal, the twin of the second is a verb about going under water, the third has two twins, one meaning at no cost and one naming a tall plant, the fourth's twin is a light wind, and the fifth's twin is where a fox sleeps. Only one of those twins could take the slot beside it and still leave a working sentence; on the page the others betray themselves. Aloud there is no such protection, so a substitution costs you the word, not merely the accent.
fields.excerpt: Each answer sits one consonant away from a rival word; pick the one that fits the sentence.
fields.focus_en:
I think the boat will sink.
Three of them were free by then.
fields.instruction: Each sentence below is missing one word. In every case another English word sits one consonant away from the answer, and in one of the five that rival would fill the slot without breaking the sentence at all, so meaning has to decide it. Read the whole line, work out what it must say, and write the word that says it. Afterwards read both candidates aloud. This exercise is really about the mouth rather than the page: if the two come out sounding identical, the gap is not yet solved.
fields.items_en:
1. The ice looked far too ___ to walk on, so we went round the lake.
2. I ___ the shop closes at six, but you should check the sign.
3. There were only ___ people waiting at the bus stop.
4. It was hard to ___ in the hot, smoky room.
5. We finished the washing-up, and ___ we sat down.
fields.subject: pronunciation

title: The missing second word: complete each two-part verb

fields.answer_note: Items one and two are a pair of opposites: the particle in the first lifts the body out of bed, the one in the second lowers it onto a seat, and neither verb states that direction by itself. Items three and four take particles that seem to be a matched pair, yet the sentences are not opposites of each other. In the third, the clue is that the programme has ended, so the particle must be the one that stops a machine working. In the fourth, a different verb takes the particle that places a garment over the body; it is written like the particle that starts a machine running, but here it describes position, not power. The fifth is the item learners most often lose: that particle changes simple seeing into searching.
fields.excerpt: Supply the small word that completes each two-part verb; the rest of the sentence tells you which.
fields.focus_en: She gets up at seven and turns on the kettle. Then she looks for her phone.
fields.instruction: Each sentence below has lost the small word that follows the verb. Write only that missing word, nothing else. The rest of the sentence always tells you which one is needed, so read to the end before you decide: the clue lies in what is happening around the verb, not in the verb itself.
fields.items_en:
1. Every day I get ___ at six, an hour before anyone else in the house.
2. Please come in, sit ___ and make yourself comfortable.
3. The film has finished, so could you turn ___ the television?
4. She put ___ her heavy coat because it was snowing outside.
5. I am looking ___ my keys, because I cannot find them anywhere.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs

title: Numbers in words: get the ending and the hyphen right

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 3 ask for figures in the 13 to 19 range; items 2, 4 and 5 need a multiple of 10, in the last pair of them inside a compound. The whole set turns on the pair of endings. In speech the ending of the 13 to 19 word has the longer vowel and closes on a consonant the other ending lacks, and said on its own the first carries its beat on the ending, the second on the syllable in front. In quick speech that consonant is swallowed and only the beat is left, which is why learners write the wrong form. Watch the spelling in items 2 and 4: in item 2 the multiple of 10 drops a letter that both its unit and the 13 to 19 word built on that unit keep, and in item 4 it adds a single letter to the unit. In items 4 and 5 the hyphen is compulsory.
fields.excerpt: Write each figure out in letters, getting the ending and the hyphen right.
fields.focus_en:
My daughter is thirteen and my son is thirty-one.
The flat costs seventy-five pounds a week.
fields.instruction: Each sentence has a gap with a figure in brackets beside it. Write that figure out in letters, exactly as you would in a sentence of your own. Where the figure lies between 21 and 99, the answer is a single hyphenated word: neither a pair of separate words with a space between them, nor the halves run together with nothing between them. Give the missing word only, and leave the brackets and the rest of the sentence as they are.
fields.items_en:
1. My sister is ___ (13), and my mother is thirty-nine.
2. The village school has only ___ (40) pupils this year.
3. I waited ___ (15) minutes for the bus, not fifty.
4. My grandmother turned ___ (81) in April.
5. The concert hall seats ___ (99) people.
fields.subject: vocabulary

title: Rewrite the action as a noun

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 4 both add an ending to the verb and both stand behind a possessive, which is the neatest compromise available: the sentence compresses, but the reader can still see who acted. Item 2 adds a single consonant rather than a whole syllable, and because the result looks so unlike a typical noun of this kind, learners often abandon it and reach for a longer synonym instead. Items 3 and 5 take two endings that recur constantly in academic writing, and the second of them shifts a consonant in the stem as it goes. Compare the two sentences in each item and watch what happens to the information: the second version is shorter, denser and more formal, but the agent can vanish completely. Examiners reward the compression and penalise the fog, so keep at least one visible agent in every paragraph.
fields.excerpt: Restate the action in each sentence as a noun, the move that lifts an essay's register.
fields.focus_en:
Heavy investment in rail transformed the network within a decade.
The sharp rise in fuel prices last winter hit rural households hardest.
fields.instruction: Each item gives you two sentences. The first states an action using a verb; the second says the same thing again but needs that action as a noun, and the noun is missing. Write only the missing noun, and build it from the verb in the first sentence rather than choosing a word that merely means something similar. This compression is what lifts the register of an exam essay - but it also buries the person doing the acting, so reach for it deliberately rather than everywhere.
fields.items_en:
1. The committee decided quickly. Its quick ___ surprised everyone.
2. The city has grown steadily since 2010. That steady ___ has put real pressure on housing.
3. The first trial failed. The ___ of the first trial delayed the project by a year.
4. The board refused to fund the pilot. The board's ___ to fund the pilot ended the discussion.
5. The company expanded into Asia last year. Its ___ into Asia has already changed the balance of its revenue.
fields.subject: exams

title: Refusing a request without causing offence

fields.answer_note: Item 1 keeps the door open by turning the refusal into a question about what could be arranged instead; the two little words in front of the gap form a fixed pair that widens the question, and a near synonym after them makes it sound as though effort, rather than availability, is the obstacle. Item 2 blames circumstances rather than unwillingness, which makes it the safest formula for a first reply to someone you do not know well. Item 3 is an image: you are not refusing, something outside you is preventing you, and the noun and the participle are locked together. Item 4 is by some distance the most formal of the five and belongs in a letter or in a decision that cannot be reversed - used in ordinary email it sounds cold and final. Item 5 answers a request the writer has just restated, and the missing word is the one softener here that can stand alone in front of a bare negative.
fields.excerpt: Complete the fixed phrases that let a work email say no without giving offence.
fields.focus_en:
Thank you for thinking of us, but unfortunately the budget for this year has already been allocated.
We would be glad to look at this again once the new financial year begins.
fields.instruction: Every line below refuses something in a work email. English softens a refusal with fixed phrases, not with polite words scattered anywhere, so exactly one word completes each phrase: write it in the gap. A bare negative is grammatically perfect and still reads as rude, which is why these formulas are worth learning whole rather than assembling from meaning.
fields.items_en:
1. Would it be at all ___ to look at the first week of March instead?
2. Unfortunately we're not in a ___ to take this on before the new quarter.
3. I would love to help, but my hands are ___ until the new budget is approved.
4. We very much ___ that we are unable to help you on this occasion.
5. You asked whether we could squeeze you in this week - I'm ___ not.
fields.subject: business

title: Grant the point first: complete each opening

fields.answer_note: Item 1 opens with an adverb of degree rather than a conjunction; the ordinary concessive conjunction would be perfectly grammatical there, but it flattens the effect the writer is after. In item 2 the frame is a fixed pair of little words standing in front of the noun phrase, and the missing half is the quantifier - nothing else can sit between the preposition and the possessive. Item 3 is frozen whole: a bare verb at the front, a modal stranded at the end, and the missing piece is the same small link that item 1 also depends on; not one part of it can be reordered. Items 4 and 5 are set openers you meet constantly in argument and in reporting - the first preserves an old subjunctive form of the verb of being, and the second uses the demonstrative that points away from the speaker, back at the concession just made, not the one you would use for something close at hand. In all five the concession is placed first on purpose, so that the clause after the comma lands as the real argument.
fields.excerpt: Complete the fixed frames that grant the other side a point before taking it back.
fields.focus_en:
Late though the hour was, nobody showed any sign of leaving.
Whatever the merits of the plan, the timing was indefensible.
fields.instruction: Each sentence grants the other side a point and then takes it straight back. The opening of that concession is a fixed frame, and one word of that frame is missing: write that single word in the gap. The all-purpose conjunction you would normally reach for fits none of these frames, and that is exactly the point - the marked opening is what gives the clause after it its weight.
fields.items_en:
1. ___ as I would like to agree with her, the figures simply do not support the claim.
2. For ___ its surface polish, the report tells us nothing we did not already know.
3. Try ___ he might, he could not get the committee to reconsider.
4. ___ that as it may, the decision has already been taken.
5. ___ said, I would not want to overstate the danger.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Put back the missing word in the fixed expression

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 2 both say that something was easy while items 3, 4 and 5 say the opposite, yet you cannot borrow a noun from one and drop it into another: each expression is stored whole. Item 3 is a deliberately painful comparison, and it is the plural that is fixed - the singular there would sound like a trip to the dentist rather than a complaint. Item 4 describes a problem that resists you; the adjective in front has a little freedom, the noun has none. If you tried a perfect synonym anywhere in these five and it felt wrong before you could explain why, that instinct is precisely what this exercise is training.
fields.excerpt: Put back the locked noun in each set expression for something easy or difficult.
fields.focus_en:
The exam itself was a walk in the park, but the interview afterwards was another matter.
Getting a straight answer out of the supplier was an uphill struggle.
fields.instruction: Each sentence ends with a set expression about how easy or how difficult something is. The verb in these expressions changes tense freely, but the noun inside them is locked: write the missing noun in the gap. If you put a perfect synonym there instead, the expression does not become slightly odd - it stops existing.
fields.items_en:
1. I was dreading the test, but it turned out to be a piece of ___.
2. The first week was chaotic, but after that it was plain ___.
3. Persuading him to change his mind was like pulling ___.
4. The second question in the exam was a hard ___ to crack.
5. Finishing all of this by Friday is a tall ___.
fields.subject: idioms

title: Passing on a claim you do not vouch for

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 5 begin with an empty subject that carries no meaning at all: it holds the subject position open so that the reported clause can arrive at the end, where the reader expects the news. Item 2 looks identical but reports the existence of something, and existence takes the other empty subject - the two are not interchangeable, and swapping them produces a sentence no native writer would accept. In items 3 and 4 the subject of the reported clause has been lifted forward into the reporting frame, so what follows is an infinitive rather than a full clause; item 4 needs one extra auxiliary because the resignations happened before the report was made. The participles differ across the five items - one is neutral, one belongs to insider briefing, one carries a legal accusation - but every one of them removes the source, which is the whole reason these structures dominate press reporting and internal briefings.
fields.excerpt: Supply the small grammatical word that lets a sentence pass on a claim without endorsing it.
fields.focus_en:
It is now generally accepted that the original forecast was far too optimistic.
The company is said to have known about the fault for several months.
fields.instruction: Each sentence passes on a claim while quietly declining to vouch for it. One small grammatical word is missing: an empty subject, the link into the infinitive, or the word that introduces the reported clause. Write that single word in the gap. Notice that no source is ever named - in this register that is deliberate, not careless.
fields.items_en:
1. ___ is widely assumed that the two firms will merge before the summer.
2. ___ is thought to be little appetite in the department for another restructuring.
3. The finance director is believed ___ have approved the payments himself.
4. Two board members are understood to ___ resigned shortly before the audit began.
5. It is alleged ___ the figures were adjusted after the deadline had passed.
fields.subject: business

title: Choosing the right present ending

fields.answer_note: Items 1, 3 and 4 have a subject that is one other person or thing, so the verb needs its special ending - and in item 4 the ending needs an extra letter because of the final sound of the verb. Items 2 and 5 have other subjects, so the verb stays in its base form.
fields.excerpt: Choose the present ending by deciding whether the subject is one other person or thing.
fields.focus_en:
She works in a hospital.
They work in the same office.
fields.instruction: Write the verb in brackets in the correct present form. First find the subject of the sentence and decide whether it is one other person or thing, or not - that decides the ending.
fields.items_en:
1. My brother ___ football every Saturday. (play)
2. I ___ to school by bus. (go)
3. She ___ English and a little Spanish. (speak)
4. My dad ___ TV after dinner. (watch)
5. My parents ___ in a small village. (live)
fields.subject: grammar

title: One thing or many: which opener fits

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 4 name a single thing, so they take the singular form. Items 2, 3 and 5 name more than one, so they take the plural form. Item 5 is the trap: the phrase begins with a little word that looks singular, but the noun it introduces is plural - count the noun, not the first word.
fields.excerpt: Decide whether the noun after the gap names one thing or several, then pick the matching opener.
fields.focus_en:
There is a bakery on our street.
There are two banks near the station.
fields.instruction: Look at the noun phrase after each gap and decide whether it names one thing or more than one. Then complete the gap with the matching form of the verb.
fields.items_en:
1. There ___ a big supermarket in my town.
2. There ___ three bedrooms in our flat.
3. There ___ some apples in the kitchen.
4. There ___ a good film on TV tonight.
5. There ___ a lot of people at the market today.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Shifting the verb back when reporting

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 5 move a present form back to a past form. In item 2 only the auxiliary sits in the gap, and it moves from present to past. In item 3 a past form steps a stage further back, to the past perfect. In item 4 the future auxiliary is replaced by its past equivalent.
fields.answers_en:
1. worked
2. were
3. had lost
4. would call
5. lived
fields.excerpt: Move the verb one step back in time when passing on what someone said.
fields.focus_en:
"I need more time," he said.
He said that he needed more time.
fields.instruction: Each item first gives the speaker's original words, then the same information passed on later. Fill the gap by moving the verb one step back in time.
fields.items_en:
1. "I work in a bank," he said. He said that he ___ in a bank.
2. "We are waiting outside," they said. They said that they ___ waiting outside.
3. "I lost my keys," she said. She told me that she ___ her keys.
4. "I will call you later," he said. He said that he ___ me later.
5. "My brother lives in Canada," she said. She said that her brother ___ in Canada.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Building the regular past

fields.answer_note: Item 1 simply adds the regular ending. Item 2 doubles its final consonant first. Items 3 and 5 change their final letter before the ending. Item 4 already ends with the letter the ending begins with, so it only adds one more letter.
fields.excerpt: Build the regular past form, watching the spelling changes that happen before the ending.
fields.focus_en:
We watched a film last night.
She studied for the test all weekend.
fields.instruction: Write the past form of the verb in brackets. All the verbs here are regular, but watch the spelling - some verbs change before the ending is added.
fields.items_en:
1. Yesterday I ___ my grandmother. (visit)
2. The bus ___ just in front of the school. (stop)
3. She ___ biology at university. (study)
4. They ___ in Rome for ten years. (live)
5. He ___ to open the window, but it was stuck. (try)
fields.subject: grammar

title: Two-part verbs: where does the pronoun go

fields.answer_note: Items 1 to 4 use separable combinations, and because the object is a pronoun it must go between the verb and its particle - placing it after the particle would be wrong. Item 5 is an inseparable combination, so the pronoun stays after both parts.
fields.answers_en:
1. turn it down
2. take them off
3. look it up
4. fill it in
5. get over it
fields.excerpt: Put the two-part verb and its pronoun object in the only order English allows.
fields.focus_en:
Turn it off before you leave.
I'll pick you up at the airport.
fields.instruction: Put the two-part verb and the small object word in brackets into the correct order to fill the gap. Think about whether this particular combination lets the object sit between its two parts or not.
fields.items_en:
1. The music is very loud - please ___ . (turn down / it)
2. Your shoes are wet, so ___ before you come in. (take off / them)
3. I don't know this word, so I will ___ later. (look up / it)
4. This form is important, so please ___ carefully. (fill in / it)
5. It was a hard week, but you will ___ soon. (get over / it)
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs

title: Dramatic negative openings: rebuild the sentence

fields.answer_note: Every answer puts an auxiliary in front of the subject. In item 1 the perfect auxiliary moves forward. In items 2 and 5 the verb has no auxiliary of its own, so a form of the dummy auxiliary is added and the main verb stays in its base form. In item 3 the verb itself moves in front of the subject because it never needs a helper. In item 4 the modal and the subject simply change places.
fields.answers_en:
1. have we
2. does she watch
3. was he
4. must you open
5. did they discover
fields.excerpt: Rebuild each sentence after its dramatic negative opening, putting the auxiliary before the subject.
fields.focus_en:
Never have I heard such nonsense.
Not only did they arrive late, but they also left early.
fields.instruction: Rebuild the missing part of each sentence using the words in brackets. After the negative opening, the auxiliary must come before the subject - add an auxiliary yourself where the verb does not have one.
fields.items_en:
1. Never ___ seen so much snow in April. (we / have)
2. Rarely ___ a film more than once these days. (she / watch)
3. Not only ___ late for the meeting, but he also forgot the report. (he / be)
4. Under no circumstances ___ this door during the flight. (you / must / open)
5. Not until the next morning ___ the truth. (they / discover)
fields.subject: grammar

title: The two all-purpose verbs: pick the right one

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 3 describe tasks or activities, so they use the activity verb. Items 2, 4 and 5 describe creating or producing something, so they use the production verb. Also check the form: items 2 and 5 need the third-person present ending, and items 3 and 4 need the past form.
fields.excerpt: Pick the right all-purpose verb for each collocation and put it in the correct form.
fields.focus_en:
I did my homework and then made dinner.
Try not to make the same mistake twice.
fields.instruction: Each gap needs one of the two verbs shown in the model sentences. Choose the right one for the collocation and put it in the correct form for the time and subject of the sentence.
fields.items_en:
1. I always ___ my homework after school.
2. She ___ a lot of mistakes when she speaks fast.
3. Yesterday we ___ the shopping together.
4. He ___ dinner for us last night.
5. Every morning she ___ her bed before breakfast.
fields.subject: vocabulary

title: Real conditions, real results: fill the gaps

fields.answer_note: Items 1, 3 and 5 sit inside the condition, so they use a present form even though the meaning is future - and item 5 also needs the third-person ending. Items 2 and 4 sit inside the result, so they use the future auxiliary plus the base verb.
fields.answers_en:
1. miss
2. will get
3. leave
4. will go
5. loses
fields.excerpt: Complete real conditions and their results, using the right form in each half of the sentence.
fields.focus_en:
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home.
If you ask her nicely, she will help you.
fields.instruction: Complete each sentence with the verb in brackets. First decide whether the gap sits in the condition half or the result half of the sentence, because the two halves use different verb forms.
fields.items_en:
1. If we ___ the last bus, we will take a taxi. (miss)
2. She ___ the job if she does well in the interview. (get)
3. If you ___ now, you will catch the train. (leave)
4. If the weather is nice on Sunday, we ___ to the beach. (go)
5. If he ___ his phone again, his parents will be angry. (lose)
fields.subject: grammar

title: Which of the three ending sounds do you hear

fields.answer_note: In items 1 and 4 the verb stem ends in a voiceless sound, so the ending is the short voiceless one. In items 2 and 5 the stem ends in a voiced sound, so the ending is the short voiced one. In item 3 the stem already ends in one of the two special stop sounds, so the ending becomes a full extra syllable - the only case where you hear an extra beat.
fields.excerpt: Say each past verb aloud and identify which of the three ending sounds you hear.
fields.focus_en:
I worked late, then I stayed in and rested.
It rained all day, so we stopped the game and waited inside.
fields.instruction: Say each sentence aloud and listen to the ending of its past verb. Choose which of the three labels in brackets matches the final sound you hear, and type that label exactly as your answer.
fields.items_en:
1. Last night we watched a film. - ___ (t / d / id)
2. She cleaned the kitchen this morning. - ___ (t / d / id)
3. They wanted to go home early. - ___ (t / d / id)
4. I helped my dad in the garden. - ___ (t / d / id)
5. He played tennis on Saturday. - ___ (t / d / id)
fields.subject: pronunciation

title: Connecting your ideas: choose the linker

fields.answer_note: Item 1 sets up a contrast between two opposite qualities. Item 2 gives the result of the first sentence. Item 3 adds a second advantage to the first one. Item 4 introduces a concrete example of the general statement. Item 5 signals that the writer is summing up - the typical move for a final paragraph.
fields.answers_en:
1. However
2. As a result
3. In addition
4. For example
5. In conclusion
fields.excerpt: Work out the logical relationship between two ideas and choose the connector that signals it.
fields.focus_en:
Travelling by plane is fast. However, it is bad for the environment.
Our city has serious traffic problems. As a result, air quality is getting worse.
fields.instruction: Each item offers two connectors in brackets. Decide what the logical relationship between the two ideas is - contrast, result, addition, example or conclusion - and fill the gap with the connector that signals it.
fields.items_en:
1. City life is exciting. ___, it can also be very stressful. (However / Therefore)
2. He didn't study at all. ___, he failed the exam. (As a result / In addition)
3. Regular exercise improves your health. ___, it helps you sleep better. (In addition / However)
4. Many capital cities are trying to cut traffic in their centres. ___, Paris has closed several big streets to cars. (For example / However)
5. ___, I believe the advantages are greater than the disadvantages. (In conclusion / For example)
fields.subject: exams

title: Present perfect or past simple?

fields.answer_note: Item 1 is a routine, so the present simple does the job. Item 2 names a finished time, which forces the past simple. Item 3 matters now - the result is on the table - and that is exactly what the present perfect is for.
fields.excerpt: Decide whether each sentence needs the present perfect or the past simple, then check the answers.
fields.focus_en:
I have finished my homework.
I finished my homework an hour ago.
fields.instruction: Choose the right form for each sentence, then open the answers to check yourself.
fields.items_en:
1. She ___ (go) to school every day.
2. They ___ (finish) the project last week.
3. I ___ (finish) - you can look at it now.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Read the strength of a soft objection: complete the softening word

fields.answer_note: Every one of these is a rejection. Item 1 is the most formal frame in the set and usually introduces a flat contradiction of what was just said. Item 2 announces disagreement while pretending to ask permission for it. Item 3 says the work will have to be redone. Item 4 closes the topic; the promised return rarely happens. Item 5 sends the proposal back for revision without saying what is wrong with it. Answer each by conceding and offering to rework, never by defending the original.
fields.excerpt: Five polite sentences from a senior colleague, each hiding a firm no behind one missing softening word.
fields.focus_en:
I'm not sure that's quite what we had in mind.
Shall we park that for now and come back to it?
fields.instruction: Each sentence is a senior colleague objecting to a proposal in the softest possible wording. One word of the fixed softening frame is missing. Write that single word, then open the answers to see how firm each objection really was.
fields.items_en:
1. With ___, I think the figures tell a rather different story.
2. I'd want to ___ back on the timing, if I may.
3. That's not ___ what we had in mind.
4. Shall we ___ that for now and revisit it next quarter?
5. It might be worth a ___ look before we commit to anything.
fields.subject: business

title: Say the place name: choose the spoken form

fields.answer_note: Items 1 and 2 belong to the family that swallows its written middle syllable, so the spoken name has two syllables where the spelling shows three. Item 3 shrinks its ending and silences the w. Item 4 ends in a weak vowel, never a hard consonant, whatever the spelling suggests. Item 5 is an unrelated word that only shares its spelling with the everyday verb for books; its first syllable is the colour red.
fields.excerpt: Five sentences with a British place name in each; pick the respelling local speakers actually use.
fields.focus_en:
We changed trains at Leicester.
The meeting is in Reading on Thursday.
fields.instruction: Each sentence names a British town or district. Two respellings are printed in brackets at the end of the line: one is how local speakers say the name, the other is how the spelling tempts you to read it. Type the correct respelling exactly as it is printed, capital letters included.
fields.items_en:
1. We changed trains at Leicester. ___ (LES-ter / LIE-ches-ter)
2. The cathedral in Worcester is worth the detour. ___ (WOR-ses-ter / WUSS-ter)
3. Her family comes from Norwich. ___ (NOR-wich / NORR-ij)
4. The festival in Edinburgh runs all August. ___ (ED-in-bruh / ED-in-burg)
5. Our office moved from London to Reading. ___ (REED-ing / RED-ing)
fields.subject: pronunciation

title: To do something wrong and escape the punishment it deserved

fields.excerpt: A three-part verb for doing something wrong and escaping the consequences; it never splits.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Do you really think you can ___ handing the report in a week late?
fields.word_collocations_en:
get away with murder
get away with it
get away with a warning
get away with cheating
fields.word_examples_en:
The auditors discovered that the directors had got away with falsifying the accounts for nearly a decade.
You might get away with a thin introduction, but examiners never forgive a missing conclusion.
fields.word_usage_note: This three-part verb means to do something wrong, risky or careless and yet escape the punishment, criticism or consequences it deserved. Two points of grammar matter at this level. First, the chunk is completely inseparable: the object always follows all three words, even when it is a pronoun. Learners who have mastered splitting two-part verbs often try to split this one as well, and the result is simply wrong. Second, the final element is a preposition, so what follows must be a noun phrase or the -ing form of a verb, never a bare infinitive. In register it runs from informal to neutral; in a formal report, a single-word verb of similar meaning usually reads better.

title: Treating a complicated question as if it had one easy answer

fields.excerpt: An adjective that always criticises: it accuses an answer of ignoring the real complexity.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Blaming the collapse on one bad decision is ___; four separate failures had to line up first.
fields.word_collocations_en:
a simplistic view of
an overly simplistic explanation
dangerously simplistic
a simplistic reading of the evidence
fields.word_examples_en:
The minister's answer was simplistic: it named one cause and ignored the three the report had documented.
Calling the dispute a clash of cultures is simplistic, and it lets both governments off the hook.
fields.word_usage_note: This adjective is never neutral, and that is what learners miss. It looks like a longer, more academic version of the ordinary word for something that is not complicated, so it turns up in essays where the writer means that an explanation was clear and economical. It says the opposite. It accuses an argument of cutting away the parts of a problem that made the problem difficult, leaving an answer that is tidy, easy and wrong. Reserve it for criticism of a policy, a headline or somebody else's reasoning. Applied to your own summary it does not read as modesty; it reads as an admission that the summary does not hold.

title: Feeling slightly unwell, but not ill enough to see a doctor

fields.excerpt: An idiom for feeling mildly unwell, with nothing to do with the forecast.
fields.subject: idioms
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. He missed yesterday's meeting because he was feeling ___.
fields.word_collocations_en:
feel under the weather
a bit under the weather
look under the weather
still under the weather
fields.word_examples_en:
She's been under the weather since the weekend, so she's working from home.
I'd rather not come out tonight, because I'm feeling a bit under the weather.
fields.word_usage_note: This three-word expression describes a mild, temporary physical state, and the noun that closes it has nothing to do with rain, sun or forecasts. Keep it for small complaints: a cold, a headache, the morning after too little sleep. Applied to a serious diagnosis it sounds oddly light, almost as though you were making a joke of the illness. Grammatically it behaves like a state rather than an action: it follows a linking verb of state rather than an action verb, and it is never placed in front of a noun the way an ordinary adjective would be. Speakers also choose it precisely because it is vague, since it explains an absence without handing over any medical detail.

title: To carry more weight than a competing consideration

fields.excerpt: The formal verb of written argument for saying one consideration matters more than another.
fields.subject: exams
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. For most students, the benefits of studying abroad far ___ the drawbacks.
fields.word_collocations_en:
far outweigh the risks
clearly outweigh the costs
the advantages outweigh the disadvantages
outweigh any short-term gain
fields.word_examples_en:
The long-term benefits of the reform clearly outweigh its short-term costs.
The damage caused by mass tourism outweighs the income it generates.
fields.word_usage_note: This verb belongs to formal written argument: it states that one consideration is more important than the one it is set against, so the balance tips in its favour. It is a core item for IELTS Task 2 and for Cambridge B2 First and C1 Advanced essays, and it is equally common in academic writing, newspaper editorials and official reports; speakers rarely reach for it in relaxed conversation. Word order carries the whole claim: the heavier consideration comes before the verb and the one it overrides comes after, so swapping the two nouns reverses your argument - and the heavier consideration can just as easily be a harm as a benefit, as sentence 2 shows. Sentence 1 hides the agreement trap: a singular noun sits between the head noun of the subject and the verb, but agreement follows the plural head noun, so the verb takes no ending; sentence 2 has a singular subject and therefore takes the third-person singular ending, and examiners notice that slip immediately. In the practice line, the degree adverb just before the gap is the most frequent intensifier used with this verb.

title: To waste time on small fiddly things instead of the job

fields.excerpt: British, informal and affectionately impatient: wasting time on fiddly things instead of the job.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. We spent the whole morning ___ around with the seating plan.
fields.word_collocations_en:
stop faffing around
faff about with the settings
faffing around for hours
a bit of a faff
fields.word_examples_en:
Stop faffing around and get in the car - we're already late.
He faffed about with the projector for twenty minutes while forty people waited.
fields.word_usage_note: British, informal, and spoken far more than written - friends, family, and colleagues you know well. Never send it to a client. The tone is impatient but affectionate: it teases someone for fussing over small, fiddly details instead of getting on with the job, and it is not an insult. Two different particles can follow the verb with no change of meaning, and both are shown in the examples. Many American listeners will not recognise it at all, so keep it for British company. A noun form of the same word also exists, used with an article, for a task that turns out to be far more trouble than it is worth.

title: Physically relaxed, or free from worry

fields.excerpt: One adjective with a physical sense and a mental sense, and a pronunciation that drops a syllable.
fields.subject: pronunciation
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. I'm not ___ with the decision, but I'll go along with it.
fields.word_collocations_en:
feel comfortable
comfortable with the decision
make yourself comfortable
a comfortable margin
fields.word_examples_en:
These shoes look heavy, but they're surprisingly comfortable.
I'm not comfortable signing anything until the lawyer has read it.
fields.word_usage_note: One word covers two senses: the physical one, used of a chair, a bed or a pair of shoes that give the body ease, and the mental one, being untroubled by a situation or a decision, which is followed by a preposition. The word itself is neutral and fits any situation, formal or casual. Now the reason it appears here, which is the pronunciation. The spelling has four syllables, but almost nobody says four: one of the vowels in the middle of the word is simply not pronounced, so the word comes out with three. British and American speakers drop a different one, which is why you will hear two slightly different versions, both correct and both three beats long. What matters for you is the rhythm rather than which version you copy: heavy stress on the first syllable, then everything after it light and fast. Giving all four written syllables equal weight is the clearest sign of a non-native speaker here.

title: To force something into a space or schedule too small for it

fields.excerpt: A mildly humorous verb for forcing something into a space or schedule that is too small for it.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Two extra interviews were ___ the schedule at the last minute.
fields.word_collocations_en:
shoehorn something into the schedule
shoehorned into the budget
shoehorn a reference into an essay
shoehorned in at the last minute
fields.word_examples_en:
They shoehorned a fourth interview into an afternoon that was already full.
The sequel shoehorns a romance into what was a perfectly good thriller.
fields.word_usage_note: Informal, mildly humorous, and everywhere in office talk and journalism. The verb always carries a criticism: the thing does not really fit and does not really belong, and someone forced it in anyway. It is almost never used on its own - name the thing being forced, then the preposition that marks movement inside, then the space that is too small for it; when the space is already obvious from the context, the shortened form of that preposition still has to be there. The passive is at least as common as the active, because the person who did the forcing is usually left unnamed.

title: Appearing to be the reason, though probably not the real one

fields.excerpt: An adverb that reports the official reason while signalling that the writer does not believe it.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. The regulation was introduced ___ to protect small investors, though its main effect has been to shield the banks.
fields.word_collocations_en:
ostensibly neutral
ostensibly to discuss
ostensibly independent
ostensibly on the grounds that
fields.word_examples_en:
The commission was set up ostensibly to improve transparency, but its findings were never published.
He was in Geneva ostensibly on holiday, though he spent every afternoon at the bank.
fields.word_usage_note: This adverb does two things at the same time: it reports the reason that was officially given, and it quietly signals that the writer does not accept that reason as the true one. Two neighbouring adverbs sit close to it but are not the same - one of them leaves the writer half-convinced that the appearance is genuine, and the other is blunter, openly sceptical, and belongs to speech. This one is the cool, formal option: it withholds agreement without ever saying so, which is why it lives in journalism, academic argument and official reports and is almost never heard in casual conversation. It usually stands immediately before the stated purpose or the stated quality, and the rest of the sentence then undercuts it.

title: To use what you already have to gain an advantage

fields.excerpt: The corporate verb for using an asset or position you already have to gain more from a situation.
fields.subject: business
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. The company plans to ___ its existing customer base to sell the new service.
fields.word_collocations_en:
leverage existing resources
leverage your network
leverage customer data
leverage a strong brand
fields.word_examples_en:
The startup leveraged its social media following to launch the new product.
We should leverage our partnership with the university to recruit graduates.
fields.word_usage_note: A corporate-register verb for using an asset, skill, relationship, or position you already have to gain more from a situation. It grew out of the noun for the mechanical advantage a long bar gives you, passed through finance, and is now everywhere in business writing and presentations. Be aware that some readers hear it as empty jargon: in plain prose a simple verb meaning to make good use of something often lands better, and outside business contexts it can sound pretentious.

title: To think of an idea, plan, or answer

fields.excerpt: The everyday three-part verb for producing an idea, a plan or an answer.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Nobody could ___ a good name for the new product.
fields.word_collocations_en:
come up with a solution
come up with an idea
come up with the money
come up with an answer
fields.word_examples_en:
We need to come up with a better plan by Friday.
She came up with the idea during her morning run.
fields.word_usage_note: A three-part verb that never separates: the object always follows the complete three-word chain. It is extremely frequent at work and in study contexts whenever someone produces an idea, a plan, a solution, an answer, or the money for something. Only the first word changes in the past. It sounds natural in speech and neutral writing; a very formal report might swap it for a single verb of Latin origin.

title: To take something you will give back later

fields.excerpt: The verb for the person who takes something for a while; the giver's side uses a different verb.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. I forgot my umbrella - can I ___ yours?
fields.word_collocations_en:
borrow money
borrow a book from the library
borrow someone's phone
fields.word_examples_en:
Can I borrow your pen for a minute?
She borrowed some money from her brother.
fields.word_usage_note: This verb belongs to the person who takes: you receive something for a short time and you must give it back. The giver's side of the same exchange uses a completely different verb, and swapping the two is one of the most common mistakes at this level - if the thing is moving toward you, this is your verb. Example 2 shows how to mention the person who gives it to you.

title: Anyone with an interest in how a project turns out

fields.excerpt: Core project vocabulary for anyone with an interest in how something turns out.
fields.subject: business
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Before we change the policy, we should hear from every ___ involved.
fields.word_collocations_en:
key stakeholders
consult stakeholders
internal and external stakeholders
stakeholder engagement
fields.word_examples_en:
We'll present the new timeline to all the key stakeholders next week.
Local residents are important stakeholders in the housing project.
fields.word_usage_note: Core project and corporate vocabulary for any person or group with an interest in how something turns out - employees, customers, investors, the local community. Do not confuse it with the narrower word for someone who owns shares in a company: this one includes everyone affected, whether or not they own anything. It is near-universal in meetings, project plans, and reports, usually in the plural, and has spread into government and education documents too.

title: Disappointing, but exactly what you expected

fields.excerpt: A golf idiom for a bad outcome that is exactly what everyone expected.
fields.subject: idioms
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Long queues at the airport in July? That's par for the ___.
fields.word_collocations_en:
pretty much par for the course
that's par for the course
par for the course in this industry
fields.word_examples_en:
The flight was delayed two hours, but that's par for the course with this airline.
Another meeting that could have been an email - par for the course around here.
fields.word_usage_note: Borrowed from golf, where every course has an expected number of strokes. Saying a bad outcome matches that expectation means it is disappointing but completely normal for the situation: the train is late again, the promise is broken again.
