The tone is resigned and often ironic, commenting on a pattern rather than a one-off. It is conversational, at home in speech and informal writing, and almost always used about negatives.

title: To have enough money to buy something

fields.excerpt: A verb that almost always follows an ability word, usually in a negative sentence or a question.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. They'd love to travel more, but they can't ___ it right now.
fields.word_collocations_en:
can't afford the rent
can't afford to wait
could never afford it
fields.word_examples_en:
We can't afford a new car this year.
I can't afford to take any more time off work.
fields.word_usage_note: This verb almost never stands alone: it nearly always follows an ability word, usually in a negative sentence or in a question about whether the money is there. After it you can put a noun or the to-form of another verb. It also stretches beyond money - you can use it for time you cannot spare or a risk you cannot take.

title: To decide to do something later instead of now

fields.excerpt: A neutral two-part verb for postponing, and where its pronoun object has to go.
fields.subject: phrasal-verbs
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. We'll have to ___ the picnic until next weekend - the forecast is terrible.
fields.word_collocations_en:
put off a decision
put off going to the doctor
put the meeting off until Friday
fields.word_examples_en:
I've been putting off my visit to the dentist for months.
Don't put it off until the last minute.
fields.word_usage_note: A neutral, everyday verb for postponing, equally natural in speech and writing. It is separable: a noun object can go after both parts or between them, and a pronoun object must go between them. When the postponed thing is an action, that action takes the -ing form, never the to-form. Watch out for a second, unrelated sense - making someone lose their enthusiasm or appetite - which context usually makes clear.

title: Costing little money

fields.excerpt: The everyday adjective for a low price, and the hint of poor quality it can carry.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. This T-shirt only costs three dollars - it's really ___.
fields.word_collocations_en:
a cheap flight
cheap food
a cheap hotel
a cheap ticket
fields.word_examples_en:
The bus is cheap, so I take it to work every day.
We found a cheap hotel near the station.
fields.word_usage_note: This is the everyday, neutral adjective for a low price, and you will hear it constantly in shops, markets, and travel conversations. Be careful: it can also hint that the quality is low, so describing someone's gift or clothes with it can sound rude. When you want to sound clearly positive about a good price, English speakers often choose a different expression that praises the value instead.

title: Changing the rules after the game has started

fields.excerpt: A football idiom for complaining that someone in authority changed the target after you had aimed.
fields.subject: idioms
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. First they wanted five references, now they want ten - they keep moving the ___.
fields.word_collocations_en:
keep moving the goalposts
move the goalposts halfway through a project
accuse someone of moving the goalposts
fields.word_examples_en:
Every time we hit the target, management moves the goalposts.
The client keeps moving the goalposts, so the project is never finished.
fields.word_usage_note: The image comes from football: mid-game, someone shifts the target so a shot that would have scored now misses. Use it to complain that a person in authority - a boss, a client, an institution - changed the requirements after the work had started, making success unfairly harder. Register is informal to neutral: fine in meetings and emails, out of place in a contract. It is almost always said with irritation, often about repeated changes.

title: Avoiding a decision between two sides

fields.excerpt: An idiom for the person who refuses to commit to either side.
fields.subject: idioms
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. Stop sitting on the ___ and tell us what you really think.
fields.word_collocations_en:
sit on the fence about an issue
stop sitting on the fence
still sitting on the fence
fields.word_examples_en:
The minister sat on the fence, refusing to back either proposal.
You can't sit on the fence forever - we need your answer by Monday.
fields.word_usage_note: The picture is of someone perched on the barrier between two fields, refusing to climb down on either side. Use it for a person who will not commit to one opinion or party in a disagreement. The tone is mildly critical: it suggests avoiding responsibility rather than careful neutrality, which makes it popular in discussions and opinion writing. The form is fixed; only the verb changes for tense.

title: Able to recover quickly from something difficult

fields.excerpt: A warm, approving adjective for people, economies and materials that spring back after a blow.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: After three failed attempts, she came back and passed. She is ___.
fields.word_collocations_en:
remarkably resilient
resilient to change
a resilient economy
fields.word_examples_en:
Kids are more resilient than we think.
The local economy proved remarkably resilient during the crisis.
fields.word_usage_note: A warm, approving word. You will hear it about people who recover from illness or setbacks, about economies, and about materials that spring back into shape. It is common in job interviews and news writing, and it always carries respect.

title: Having a lot to do and no free time

fields.excerpt: The everyday adjective for a person with a lot to do or a place full of people, and the polite way to say you cannot come.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. I can't talk now - I'm ___ with a customer.
fields.word_collocations_en:
a busy day
busy at work
too busy to call
a busy road
fields.word_examples_en:
Sorry, I can't come tonight. I'm busy.
The shop is very busy at lunchtime.
fields.word_usage_note: This is the everyday adjective for a person who has a lot to do, and also for a place or a time with a lot of people and activity. It is the normal, polite way to say you cannot do something: with a short apology first, you do not need to give any other reason. It goes after the verb for being, and in front of a noun. When you say what you are busy doing, use the -ing form of the verb after it, or use the word for with and a noun.

title: So weak that it is unlikely to survive examination

fields.excerpt: The formal adjective for a link or an argument too thin to carry the weight put on it, the measured way to dismiss a claim.
fields.subject: vocabulary
fields.word_check_item_en: 1. The link between the study and the headline it produced is ___ at best.
fields.word_collocations_en:
a tenuous link
tenuous at best
a tenuous grip on power
increasingly tenuous
fields.word_examples_en:
The connection between the two events is tenuous at best.
She kept a tenuous hold on the leadership through the winter.
fields.word_usage_note: A word for connections, arguments, claims and positions that are thin, stretched and close to breaking. It belongs to formal and academic register, where it does precise work: it does not say a link is false, it says the link is too weak to bear the weight being put on it. That makes it a favourite of reviewers, examiners and journalists, who use it to dismiss an argument while sounding measured. Applied to a link or an argument it is nearly always an evaluation, and usually of someone else's reasoning; applied to a hold, a grip or a position it is simply descriptive. A fixed two-word phrase meaning at the very most often follows it, and that phrase makes the judgement harsher, not softer.

title: Coffee-machine small talk about a much-delayed office relocation

fields.check_item_en: 1. With no firm date for the move, speaker A's team have given up planning - they are just playing it by ___.
fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Oh, hello - it's Priya, isn't it? We met at the away day in March.
2. B: That's right, yeah. And you're... don't tell me. Marcus? Something in finance?
3. A: Marcus, yeah - well remembered. How are things up on the fourth floor?
4. B: Honestly? Chaotic. We're completely snowed under with the year-end reporting, and half the team's on leave.
5. A: I did hear that. Is your move still happening in October, or...?
6. B: That's the thing - it's all up in the air at the moment. They keep promising we'll know by Friday, and then Friday comes and goes.
7. A: Same story on our floor. We were told the seating plan was final, and last week they redrew the whole thing.
8. B: So how are you handling it? Are you booking desks ahead, or...
9. A: We've stopped planning altogether, honestly. We're just playing it by ear until someone tells us otherwise.
10. B: Probably the sensible option. Right, I'd better run - mine's already going cold.
11. A: Yeah, me too. Nice to put a face to the name properly, anyway.
12. B: You too. And if you hear a date before we do, let me know, will you?
fields.excerpt: Two near-strangers fill the wait at the coffee machine with small talk about a move that keeps slipping.
fields.listen_for: Three fixed expressions carry this conversation, all of them common in professional small talk. In line 4 the second speaker describes an overload of work through a weather image; in line 6 she presents an unresolved decision as if it were suspended somewhere overhead. In line 9 the first speaker uses a phrase borrowed from musicians that means improvising rather than working to a schedule - its closing word refers to a part of the body, and learners regularly swap it for a similar-sounding word to do with time. All three are neutral in register: safe in the office, natural in speech.
fields.next_label: Next: a reference table of everyday expressions where one word is frozen and cannot be swapped
fields.situation: Two colleagues from different departments, acquainted only from a single company event some months back, bump into each other at the coffee machine. While their cups fill, they exchange updates on a long-postponed office relocation and discover that neither department has been given any firm information.
fields.subject: idioms

title: Disagreeing with a colleague's plan without turning the meeting into a fight

fields.check_item_en: 1. Hmm, I take your ___. What if we split the difference, then?
fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Right, so my thinking is we bring the launch forward to March. The sooner we're out there, the better.
2. B: Mm, I can see the appeal of that, I really can. It's just that March gives us barely six weeks for testing.
3. A: True, but the testing's mostly done, isn't it? We're just polishing at this point.
4. B: The core features are solid, I'll give you that. The payment side, though, is still throwing up errors.
5. A: OK, that's... yes, that's fair. Could we launch without payments and add them in April?
6. B: We could, in theory. I'm just not sure a launch without the main selling point really counts as a launch.
7. A: Hmm, I take your point. What if we split the difference, then? Soft launch in March, full release in May.
8. B: That might actually work. I'd still want one more proper round of testing first, though.
9. A: Of course. Shall we say testing wraps up by mid-April?
10. B: Sounds reasonable. Let's put it to the rest of the team on Monday.
fields.excerpt: Two colleagues disagree about a launch date and keep the meeting from turning into an argument.
fields.listen_for: Neither speaker ever produces a flat refusal. Listen to how the second speaker builds each objection: lines 2, 4 and 6 all begin by accepting part of the other person's argument, and only then does the counterargument arrive. Notice the fixed expression the first speaker uses at the start of line 7 to concede before offering a compromise, and how doubt is voiced throughout as personal uncertainty rather than as direct contradiction. This grant-first, object-second rhythm is what makes disagreement sound professional instead of hostile.
fields.next_label: Next: the grammar of conceding before you argue back
fields.situation: Two colleagues are in a weekly planning meeting at a software company. One wants the product released earlier than planned; the other believes the schedule leaves too little time to check everything properly. They disagree about the timing, but both are determined to stop the discussion becoming an argument.
fields.subject: business

title: Ringing a company to move an appointment you cannot keep

fields.check_item_en: 1. ___ it be possible to move it?
fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Good morning, Carter and Hale, Emma speaking. How can I help?
2. B: Oh, hello. It's Daniel Rossi here. I've got an appointment with Ms Carter on Thursday, and... well, something's come up. Would it be possible to move it?
3. A: Let me have a look. Thursday at half past two, is that the one?
4. B: That's it, yes. I'm really sorry, but my flight back doesn't land until Thursday afternoon now, so I won't be able to get there.
5. A: No problem at all. She's free on Friday at ten, or in the afternoon at four. Would either of those suit you?
6. B: Friday morning's tricky... Could we say four o'clock?
7. A: Of course. So that's Friday at four instead of Thursday.
8. B: Perfect. And it's still at the Milton Road office, is it?
9. A: It is, yes. I'll send you a new confirmation this afternoon.
10. B: Great, thanks so much for your help. Bye now.
11. A: You're welcome. Goodbye.
fields.excerpt: A client rings to move an appointment his flight will make him miss; the receptionist offers alternatives.
fields.listen_for: Two things to catch. First, the caller never demands the change: in lines 2 and 6 he softens each request into a past-form modal question, which makes the imposition sound smaller. This is the standard way to ask a favour of a stranger at work; the bare present form sounds abrupt by comparison. Second, listen for the three little words that place the meeting in time: one goes before the day, another before the clock time, and a third before the part of the day. The receptionist uses all three inside a single offer in line 5.
fields.next_label: Next: making the same kind of polite request in writing
fields.situation: A client telephones a company's front desk because his return flight now lands too late for the appointment he booked. The receptionist checks the diary, offers two alternatives, and the two of them agree on a new day and time before ending the call.
fields.subject: business

title: Two friends compare their weekends on a Monday morning

fields.check_item_en: 1. On Saturday, B ___ to a friend's party and didn't get home until two.
fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Hiya! You look really tired.
2. B: Yeah, I am. We went to Sarah's party on Saturday and didn't get home till two.
3. A: Two? That's late. Was it good?
4. B: Really good. She cooked for about twenty people. What about you?
5. A: Nothing special. I stayed in on Saturday and watched a film.
6. B: Which one?
7. A: The new space one - I forgot the name. Oh, and on Sunday I took my brother to the football.
8. B: Did they win?
9. A: No, they lost two-nil. He cried all the way home, poor kid.
10. B: Oh no. Well, at least you saw a match. I just slept all Sunday.
fields.excerpt: Two friends trade weekend stories before work, one of them visibly short of sleep.
fields.listen_for: Every finished action in this exchange is in the past simple, and the two ways English forms it sit side by side. Several verbs take the regular written ending - you hear them in lines 4 and 5, and in the second verb of line 9. Others change their whole shape instead, as in lines 2, 7 and 10 - and the first verb of line 9 belongs to this group too. Notice also what happens when an auxiliary appears: in the question in line 8 and the negative in line 2, the auxiliary carries the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
fields.next_label: Next: the reference table of past forms that refuse the regular ending
fields.situation: It is Monday, the start of the working week, and two friends who work together meet before the day begins. One of them is visibly short of energy after a celebration that finished very late; the other had a much calmer two days. They ask each other about their free time.
fields.subject: grammar

title: Asking a stranger the way to the nearest pharmacy

fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Excuse me - sorry to bother you. Is there a chemist near here?
2. B: A chemist? Yes, there's one in the market square, on Mill Street.
3. A: Oh good. Is it far?
4. B: No, five minutes on foot. Go straight on to the traffic lights.
5. A: Straight on to the lights... okay.
6. B: Then turn left at the lights, and it's on your right, next to the bakery.
7. A: Left at the lights, on the right. Got it.
8. B: You can't miss it - there's a big green cross above the door.
9. A: Brilliant, thank you so much.
10. B: You're welcome. Oh - it shuts at half past five, so be quick.
fields.excerpt: A visitor asks a passer-by for the closest place to buy medicine and gets a two-step route.
fields.listen_for: The route comes as two short orders, one in line 4 and one in line 6, each built on a bare command verb with no polite padding - that is simply how directions sound in English. Around them, three small position words share the work: one places the shop inside an open area in line 2, another attaches it to a road name in line 2 and to a side in line 6, and a third pins the change of direction in line 6 and the closing time in the final line to an exact point. Notice too how the first speaker repeats each instruction in lines 5 and 7 - a checking habit worth copying whenever someone tells you the way.
fields.next_label: Next: the full scale behind those three little position words, for time and place alike
fields.situation: A visitor who does not know the town stops a passer-by to ask where the closest place to buy medicine is. The passer-by explains the short route in two steps, mentions a landmark that makes the shop easy to spot, and adds a friendly warning that it closes quite soon.
fields.subject: vocabulary

title: Buying a few things in a small shop: greeting, asking and paying

fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: Good morning.
2. B: Good morning. Can I help you?
3. A: Yes, please. Two apples and a bottle of water, please.
4. B: Here you are. Anything else?
5. A: Um... yes. A small loaf of bread, please.
6. B: Of course. So that's two apples, water and bread.
7. A: How much is that?
8. B: That's four pounds, please.
9. A: Here's five.
10. B: Thanks. And one pound change.
11. A: Thank you. Bye!
12. B: Bye. Have a nice day!
fields.excerpt: A customer greets the shopkeeper, asks for three everyday items and pays.
fields.listen_for: Two things carry the politeness here. First, the one small word the customer attaches to each request - listen for it in lines three and five, and notice the shopkeeper returning it in line eight when naming the total. Without it, the same requests sound like orders. Second, the short fixed question in line seven that asks what everything comes to: learn it as a whole phrase rather than building it word by word. Notice also how short the answers are - full sentences would sound odd across a shop counter.
fields.next_label: Next: which of the words for food take a plural, and which never do
fields.situation: A customer steps into a small neighbourhood shop to pick up three everyday items. The shopkeeper greets them, fetches what they ask for, adds everything up and takes the money. It is one of the shortest and most common exchanges in the language, and both speakers keep it brief and friendly.
fields.subject: vocabulary

title: A speaking exam: defending a view while the examiner tests it

fields.check_item_en: 1. Much ___ I sympathise with those drivers, I'd argue the figures point the other way.
fields.dialogue_en:
1. E: You argued for a complete ban. Isn't that rather sweeping, given how many people rely on their cars?
2. C: It's a fair challenge. Much as I sympathise with those drivers, I'd argue the figures point the other way: most journeys into a city centre are under three miles.
3. E: Figures can be read in several ways, though. What about tradespeople carrying equipment?
4. C: Granted, they're a genuine exception, and any sensible scheme would license them. My point is that exceptions shouldn't set the rule for everyone else.
5. E: Some would say a ban simply pushes the traffic to the suburbs.
6. C: That's often claimed, and I don't dismiss it. The evidence from cities that have tried it, however, suggests the traffic doesn't move so much as shrink.
7. E: So you're confident the public would accept it?
8. C: Confident is perhaps too strong. I'd say acceptance tends to follow implementation rather than precede it, which is why I'd start with a trial.
9. E: And if the trial failed?
10. C: Then the case would have been tested honestly, which is more than can be said for the current arrangement.
fields.excerpt: An examiner probes a candidate's position on banning cars from city centres; the candidate concedes, corrects and holds the line.
fields.listen_for: Notice that the candidate never simply says yes or no. Lines 2, 4 and 6 each open by accepting part of the examiner's challenge and only then turn the argument back. Line 2 uses the fixed concessive frame that fronts the conceded point; line 4 opens with a single-word concession before drawing the line; line 6 acknowledges the objection before producing evidence against it. Line 8 is the key move of the whole exchange: the candidate refuses the examiner's word for their own position and replaces it with a more careful one. That habit of correcting the strength of a claim, rather than accepting or denying it, is what examiners at this level are listening for.
fields.next_label: The grammar behind line 2: granting a point, then taking it back
fields.situation: The final part of a C2 speaking exam. The candidate has just spoken for two minutes on whether cities should ban private cars from their centres. The examiner now asks follow-up questions designed to test how well the candidate can hold a position, concede a point without collapsing, and keep the argument moving under pressure. The candidate is expected to sound considered rather than certain.
fields.subject: exams

title: Hearing a quiet no: a junior proposal is gently parked

fields.check_item_en: 1. Let's ___ it for now, shall we, and come back to it when the year-end is out of the way.
fields.dialogue_en:
1. A: So the idea is a single monthly dashboard instead of the four separate reports. It would save the clients time and us about a day a month.
2. P: Right. Interesting. And you've run this past the client leads?
3. A: Not yet, I wanted to bring it here first.
4. P: Mm. I can see the thinking. I'm just not sure it's quite what our larger clients are expecting from us.
5. A: I think once they saw the format they'd find it easier to use.
6. P: They might. It's probably worth a second look at how it lands with the two biggest accounts before we go any further.
7. A: Of course. Would it help if I mocked up a version for one of them?
8. P: Let's park it for now, shall we, and come back to it when the year-end is out of the way.
9. A: That makes sense. I'll hold off and pick it up in the new year.
10. P: Good. Thanks for putting the work in, though. It's the right instinct.
fields.excerpt: A partner turns down a junior analyst's proposal without ever saying no; she has to hear the refusal in the wording and step back gracefully.
fields.listen_for: The partner never says no, and never says the proposal is wrong. Listen to how the refusal builds instead: line 2 is neutral on the surface, but the one-word verdict that follows its opening word is a warning, and the question after it locates a gap in the process. Line 4 pairs a concession with the softest possible doubt. Line 6 sends the work back for revision without naming a fault. Line 8 closes the topic using the fixed phrase for shelving something; the promised return is a courtesy, not a plan. Now listen to the analyst: in line 7 she half-concedes but still offers more work, which is what draws the explicit shelving in line 8, and by line 9 she has accepted the outcome in her own words. Line 10 is the reward for reading the room correctly.
fields.next_label: Practise it: complete the softening word in five quiet objections
fields.situation: A monthly review meeting at a British consultancy. A junior analyst has prepared a proposal to change how the team reports to clients and is presenting it to the partner who runs the practice. The partner does not want the change, but will not say so directly in front of the team. The analyst has to work out, from the wording alone, that the proposal has been turned down, and then leave the meeting with her standing intact.
fields.subject: business

title: In, on, at: one scale of precision that covers both time and place

fields.body:
Every course teaches these three prepositions as three lists: one for clock times, one for days, one for months and years, and then three more lists for places. Six lists, several dozen items, no reason behind any of them. That is a great deal to memorise for something you have to decide in the middle of a sentence, at speed, several times a minute. There is a principle underneath, it covers time and place with the same move, and it removes most of the memorising.

One principle, not six lists

Think of the three as a scale of precision. The first treats what follows as a single point with no size worth mentioning. The second treats it as a surface or a line, something with extent that you sit on rather than inside. The third treats it as a container, something with an inside that surrounds you. Small point, flat surface, enclosing space: that ordering is the whole system, and English applies it to time exactly as it applies it to physical space.

I will see you at six.

I will see you on Monday.

I will see you in August.

The three lines above show the scale running from narrowest to widest. A clock time is treated as a point, so it takes the first preposition. A day is a bounded stretch you can name and sit within, so it takes the second. A month is long enough to be a container you are inside for a while, so it takes the third. Nobody had to decide these one at a time; each follows from how big the speaker treats the period as being.

The same scale for places

Now the same three, used for physical space, in the same order of increasing size.

She is at the door.

The keys are on the table.

The letter is in the drawer.

The first line treats the position as a point, a location with no interior worth mentioning; this is why the same preposition is used for addresses, bus stops and events, all of which are places you are simply present at rather than inside. The second is a surface, and the object rests on top of it. The third is a container with an inside, and the object is enclosed by it. The identical logic that put a clock time first and a month last puts a doorway first and a drawer last.

The scale explains cases that otherwise look arbitrary. A town or a country is large enough to be a container, so it takes the third preposition; a specific address is treated as a point, so it takes the first, even though the address is inside the town. Both are true at once, because the choice describes how the speaker is framing the place, not how large it really is.

Time expressions, from precise to broad

The scale gives you a default for almost every time expression you will need.

at 7.30, at midnight, at lunchtime, at the weekend

on Tuesday, on 14 March, on my birthday, on Christmas Day

in the morning, in April, in summer, in 2019, in the twenty-first century

Everything in the first line above is a point on the clock or a moment treated as one. Everything in the second is a named day or a date, which is a bounded stretch with a name. Everything in the third is a longer period that surrounds the moment you are describing, and note that the last two items show the scale still working at the size of years and centuries. Two items are worth flagging: the weekend appears in the first line here because British usage treats it as a point in the week, and North American usage puts it in the second line instead, which is one of the few places where the two varieties genuinely disagree.

There is also a small closed set of expressions that take no preposition at all, and learners often insert one out of habit. Anything beginning with the words for this, last, next or every stands on its own, and so does the word for the day before today and the day after it.

The difference between in time and on time

These two look like a free choice and are not; they say different things, and the difference matters in work English.

The train arrived on time.

We arrived in time to catch the train.

The first line above means punctual: the event happened at the moment it was scheduled to happen, and the reference point is the timetable. The second means early enough: something was achieved before a deadline passed, with room to spare, and the reference point is whatever had to be done. A train described by the second line would be a train you caught, not a train that ran punctually. The pattern holds for the pair as a whole, so a report handed in punctually uses the first and a report handed in before it was too late uses the second.

Where the principle stops

Being honest about the limits is more useful than pretending the rule is total. Prepositions are the part of English that resists systematising hardest, and there are three places where the scale runs out. Some fixed expressions simply take the preposition they take, and no reasoning recovers it. Some nouns take a preposition determined by the noun rather than by the geometry, which is why they must be learnt as pairs. And transport is a small closed system of its own, where the choice depends on whether you can stand up inside the vehicle rather than on its size.

The practical consequence is that the scale should be your default, not your only strategy. Use it to generate the answer, and treat the exceptions as vocabulary. Where a preposition is fixed by the word in front of it, the reference page listing which small word follows which common adjective is the place to learn those pairs directly, because no principle will produce them.

The mistakes that cost marks

Three errors dominate. The first is using the container preposition with a named day, which happens because a day feels like a period you are inside; the scale puts a named day on the surface instead. The second is inserting a preposition in front of the expressions that take none, which is the most frequent of all and the easiest to fix, since the list is short and closed. The third is transferring the preposition from your own language, and it is worth knowing that this is the single least transferable area of grammar between languages: two languages that agree on almost everything else will disagree here, so a direct translation is more likely to be wrong than right.

The three pieces here that go with this page are the table laying the scale out for time and place together, the lesson on the punctual and the early-enough pair, and the practice set that includes an item where no word belongs at all. Because these three words appear in nearly every sentence you write, a consistent error with them shows up everywhere, and examiners count it under grammatical accuracy rather than style. The same frequency makes them quick to practise: any paragraph you have already written contains several, and checking them takes a minute. Everything else here is arranged on the page that sorts material by level and on the page that sorts it by subject.

title: A, an, the, and none at all: how English articles actually work

fields.body:
Articles are the most frequent words in English and among the last a learner gets right. They carry almost no meaning of their own, they are unstressed and easy to miss in speech, and a sentence without them is still perfectly understandable. That combination is exactly what makes them persistent: nothing breaks when you get them wrong, so the error never corrects itself, and it goes on marking your English as non-native long after your vocabulary and your tenses have stopped doing so.

There are three choices, not two

English grammar offers two articles, and most courses stop there. In practice you are choosing between three options every time you use a noun, because leaving the article out is itself a grammatical choice with its own meaning, usually called the zero article. Learners who think there are only two options never consider the third, and so they insert something wherever a noun appears.

I bought a book.

I bought the book.

I bought books.

The three lines above are all correct, and each says something different. The first introduces one item the listener has not heard of before; the indefinite article marks the noun as non-specific, one of a kind rather than a particular one. The second refers to an item both speaker and listener can identify, which is what the definite article does. The third makes a general statement about more than one item, with no article at all. The difference between them is not politeness or formality, it is a claim about what your listener already knows.

The rules for a and an: sound, not spelling

The indefinite article has two forms, and the choice between them is decided by the first sound of the word that follows, never by the first letter. This trips up careful learners more than careless ones, because a careful learner looks at the written word.

a university, a European city, a one-way street

an hour, an honest answer, an MBA

Every item in the first line above begins with a vowel letter, and yet each takes the form used before consonant sounds, because each begins with a consonant sound the moment you say it aloud: the first two open with the gliding sound made by raising the tongue towards the roof of the mouth, and the third with the one made by rounding the lips. Every item in the second line begins with a consonant letter and takes the other form, because the first sound is a vowel sound: in the first two the opening letter is silent, and in the third the letter is pronounced as its name, which starts with a vowel. Say the word before you choose, and the rule never fails.

The same sound-before-spelling principle governs several other decisions in English, which is why the reference page on letters that are written but never spoken is worth keeping to hand. Note also that the indefinite article is singular only. It cannot appear in front of a plural noun, and it cannot appear in front of an uncountable noun, because both of those describe quantities rather than single items.

When to use the definite article

The definite article makes one claim: that the listener can work out which one you mean. Everything else follows from that. It is used with singular and plural nouns alike, and with uncountable nouns too, because identifiability has nothing to do with number.

Close the door, please.

The report you sent has arrived.

She is the tallest person in the office.

The Danube runs through four capital cities.

Each line above gives the listener a different route to the identification. In the first, the situation does it: there is one obvious door in the room. In the second, the words after the noun do it, narrowing the field to one. In the third, the superlative does it, since there can only be one tallest. In the fourth, the noun is simply unique in the world, and a small set of geographical names behaves this way. The most common route of all is not shown above, and it is mentioning the noun a second time: the first mention takes the indefinite article, every mention after it takes the definite one, because by then the listener knows which one you mean.

When to use no article at all

The zero article is the option learners forget, and it covers a great deal of ordinary English. Use no article when you are speaking in general terms about a plural noun or an uncountable noun.

Water freezes at zero degrees.

Cats sleep for most of the day.

She studies medicine at university.

We had breakfast at eight.

None of the four lines above refers to a particular item; each makes a general statement, and adding the definite article to any of them would change the meaning by narrowing it to something specific. The last two show a further group worth learning as a set: certain everyday nouns naming meals, institutions and forms of transport drop the article when you mean the ordinary activity rather than the physical building or object. Whether a noun can take the zero article at all depends on whether it is countable, so the reference table showing which everyday nouns take a plural and which never do is the companion piece to this section, and the list of plurals that refuse to follow the rule covers the forms that look singular but are not.

If your first language has no articles

Thai, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Polish and many other languages have no articles at all. If you speak one of them, the difficulty is not that the rules are complicated, it is that you are being asked to make a distinction your language never requires you to think about, several times in every sentence, at conversational speed. The information carried by an English article is usually supplied in those languages by word order, by context, or by nothing at all, because the listener works it out.

That produces a specific and very recognisable pattern: articles are omitted rather than confused. The correction is not to memorise more rules but to build the habit of asking one question every time you produce a singular countable noun, since that is the case where English never allows nothing. If your language does have articles, your error will be the opposite one, transferring your own usage into English and putting the definite article in front of general plural statements where English wants none.

How to pronounce the definite article

The definite article has two pronunciations, and they follow the same sound rule as the indefinite one. Before a consonant sound it is reduced almost to nothing, with the neutral unstressed vowel English uses everywhere in weak syllables. Before a vowel sound the vowel lengthens and the word is easier to hear. Speakers also use that longer form deliberately before any word at all when they want to emphasise it, which is why you will occasionally hear it before a consonant.

This matters less for being understood than for understanding others: the reduced form is so short in fast speech that learners listening for it often do not hear it, conclude the speaker omitted it, and take that as permission to omit it themselves.

The mistakes that cost marks

Four errors account for most of the damage in exam writing. The first is omitting the article in front of a singular countable noun, which is never correct in English and is the commonest error among speakers of article-less languages. The second is the reverse, putting the definite article in front of a general plural or uncountable statement, which turns a general truth into a claim about specific items. The third is choosing the indefinite form by letter rather than sound. The fourth is using the indefinite article with a plural or uncountable noun, which cannot happen at all.

Examiners treat all four as grammatical accuracy rather than style, and because articles appear so often, a consistent error with them affects a great many sentences on the page. That frequency cuts both ways: it makes the error costly, and it makes practice efficient, because every paragraph you write gives you a dozen chances to rehearse the choice.

What to do this week

The three pieces here that go with this page are the table of all four choices, the lesson on letting the sound decide the form, and the practice set that makes you leave the gap empty when nothing belongs there. Then take something you have already written and mark only the singular countable nouns. Every one of them needs an article or a word doing an article-like job, and for most learners that single pass finds more errors than any exercise. Then read a page aloud and listen for the reduced form in your own speech; if it is not there, your listener will not hear it either. Everything on this site is grouped on the page that sorts material by level and on the page that sorts it by subject.

title: Present perfect vs past simple: the question that actually decides it

fields.body:
Of all the choices English grammar asks an intermediate learner to make, this is the one that keeps going wrong long after the rule has been learnt. Both the past simple and the present perfect describe something that happened before now, both are taught in the same week, and the textbook explanation, that one is finished and the other is not, collapses the moment you meet a present perfect sentence about something plainly over. The rule is real, but it is usually stated backwards.

What each tense actually claims

The past simple is formed from the past form of the verb alone. The present perfect is formed from the auxiliary in its present form plus the past participle, and that auxiliary is the important part: it is a present tense verb. That is not a piece of trivia, it is the whole difference. A present perfect sentence is grammatically a statement about now that happens to mention a past event. A past simple sentence is a statement about then.

I lost my keys.

I have lost my keys.

Both lines above describe the same event, and both are correct English. The first places that event in finished time and says nothing else; it invites a follow-up question about when. The second says that the event has a present consequence, and the consequence is the point: the keys are still missing now. Speakers choose the second when the present result is what matters, and the first when the event itself is what they are reporting. Neither is more polite, more formal or more advanced than the other.

The one question that decides it

Here is the test that works in practice, and it is not about whether the action is finished. Ask instead whether the sentence locates the event in a finished stretch of time. If it does, the past simple is not merely preferred, it is obligatory, and the present perfect becomes ungrammatical.

I have seen that film last night.

I saw that film last night.

I have seen that film.

The first line above is the single most common error at this level, and it is a hard error rather than an awkward phrasing: a native speaker will not produce it. It fails because the closing time expression names a stretch of time that is over, and a tense whose auxiliary is present cannot sit inside finished time. The second line repairs it by matching the tense to the time expression. The third repairs it the other way, by removing the time reference altogether, and now means something different: it reports an experience without saying when, which is exactly what the present perfect is for.

The time expressions that force your hand

Because the choice is decided by how the sentence frames time, a small set of expressions effectively makes it for you. Learning these is more efficient than learning the abstract rule, because they appear in most of the sentences where the choice arises.

yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago, when I was a child

already, yet, so far, up to now, recently

today, this week, this year, ever, never

Every expression in the first line above names finished time and requires the past simple. Every expression in the second line points at the stretch running up to the present moment and requires the present perfect. The third line is the interesting one, because those expressions can take either tense: the period they name includes the present moment, so the speaker decides whether to treat it as still open or already closed. That is a genuine choice rather than a rule, and it is the reason two fluent speakers can describe the same morning differently.

Why your own language is working against you

If you speak French, Spanish, Italian, German or Dutch, you have a compound past form built the same way as the English present perfect, from an auxiliary plus a participle. In several of those languages that form has become the ordinary way to talk about finished events in conversation, and the older simple past survives mainly in writing. The shape maps across perfectly; the meaning does not.

So the error is not carelessness, it is a well-formed sentence in your first language translated word for word. It produces present perfect sentences everywhere a Romance or Germanic speaker would naturally use their compound past, including inside finished time, which is precisely where English forbids it. Speakers of languages with no perfect construction at all, including Slavic and most East Asian languages, make the opposite error and under-use the present perfect, reaching for the past simple even when the present consequence is the whole point.

Identify which of the two you are, because the correction is different in each case. If your language has the compound past, your task is to stop using the present perfect by default and reserve it for present relevance. If it does not, your task is to notice the situations where English expects it and use it deliberately.

Experience, duration and the unfinished present

Three situations account for most correct uses of the present perfect, and all three share the feature that the present moment is inside the picture.

She has worked here since March.

Have you ever broken a bone?

They have finished the report, so we can send it.

The first line above measures a stretch of time that began in the past and is still running: she works here now, and the sentence would be wrong if she had left. The second asks about experience at any point in a life still being lived, which is why this pattern is so common in questions to people you have just met. The third states a past action purely for its present consequence, and the second half of that line makes the consequence explicit. In all three, replacing the tense with the past simple would either change the meaning or make the sentence false.

The related form that adds the continuous, covered in the lesson on the continuous version of this tense, keeps the same present connection but shifts the attention from the completed result to the activity itself.

The mistakes that cost marks

Four errors account for most of the damage in exam writing and speaking. The first is the one shown above: a present perfect sentence carrying a finished time expression. The second is using the past simple for a situation that is still true, which quietly tells your reader the situation has ended. The third is the wrong participle, since the irregular verbs are exactly the frequent ones and the participle is often not the same word as the past form. The fourth is dropping the auxiliary in speech, which turns the sentence into a past simple with an unusual verb form and undoes the choice you correctly made.

The third of those is worth attacking directly, because it is vocabulary rather than grammar and can simply be learnt. The reference list of irregular past forms gives you the participles beside the past forms, which is the comparison that matters here. If the regular endings themselves are still slowing you down, the lesson on building the regular past covers the spelling, and the article on pronouncing that ending handles the sound.

What to do this week

Stop asking whether the action is finished, because that question does not discriminate. Ask instead whether the sentence names a finished time, and let the answer choose the tense for you. Then take your own recent writing and look only at the sentences containing a time expression: the errors cluster there, and you can usually fix a week of them in ten minutes. When you want to test the choice rather than read about it, the practice set that makes you pick between the two is built on exactly this decision. Everything else on this site is sorted by level on the page that groups material by level, and by topic on the page that groups it by subject.

title: Separable and inseparable phrasal verbs: the test that tells them apart

fields.body:
Courses hand you two lists of phrasal verbs: the separable ones, whose object can sit inside the verb, and the inseparable ones, whose object cannot. Then they tell you to memorise which verb belongs to which list, as though this were vocabulary. It is not vocabulary. The two lists are two different structures wearing identical clothes, and a single test tells them apart in about a second.

What follows is that test, worked examples of both kinds, and the thing the lists in your textbook cannot show you: why the same verb sometimes prefers one order and sometimes the other. Understand the difference in structure and you will not need the lists again.

What a phrasal verb is, and why there are two lists

A phrasal verb is a verb combined with one or two small words, where the combination works as a single verb and usually carries a meaning you could not work out from the parts on their own. That is the whole difficulty of them: the grammar is ordinary, but the meaning is not. English has several thousand, and they do most of the everyday work that a single formal verb does in careful writing.

Only some of them raise a question of word order at all. A phrasal verb that takes an object is transitive, and only transitive ones can be separable or inseparable. Many phrasal verbs are intransitive: they take no object, so nothing could sit in the middle even in principle.

The car broke down on the motorway.

She grew up in Manchester.

The plane took off an hour late.

None of the three lines above could be split, because there is no object to place anywhere. So the first question to ask about any phrasal verb is whether it takes an object at all. If it does not, there is no word-order problem to solve, and neither of the two lists applies to it.

Two structures, one appearance

The small word at the end of a two-part verb is one of two very different things. It is either a particle, which belongs to the verb and can move around the object, or a preposition, which belongs to the noun after it and cannot be separated from it. A preposition is glued to whatever follows; a particle is not glued to anything. That single structural difference is the whole of what separable and inseparable mean.

Turn off the radio.

Turn the radio off.

Turn it off.

I ran into my old teacher.

I ran into her.

In the first group the object moves freely to either side of the small word. In the second group nothing moves at all. Here is the test that separates them without any memorising: swap the object for a pronoun and try to place that pronoun in the middle. If it fits there, you have a particle and the verb is separable. If the pronoun refuses the middle and has to follow the small word, as it does in the last line of the second group, you have a preposition and that verb is inseparable.

There is a second clue for your ear. In neutral speech a particle carries stress and a preposition usually does not, so the two groups sound different even when they look the same on the page.

With a pronoun, the middle is not a choice

This is the part most courses bury, and it is the most useful thing here. Textbooks present the middle position as an option, and with an ordinary noun object it genuinely is one: the first two lines of the first group above are equally natural. With a pronoun it is not an option. A splitting verb requires its pronoun object in the middle, which is why the third line of the first group is the only possible form there. Heavy contrastive emphasis can bend this in speech, but that is a special effect, not a position you should be reaching for.

Learners who treat the position as free end up producing a word order that fluent speakers simply do not use, and because pronouns are everywhere, the error repeats in almost every sentence. Fixing this one habit does more for how natural you sound than learning another twenty of these verbs.

Separable phrasal verbs: ten worked examples

The ten numbered lines below collect some of the most common separable phrasal verbs in English, each one shown with its object already sitting in the middle. Every object here is an ordinary noun phrase, and every line is a sentence you could use today.

1. Please fill this form in before Friday.

2. She called the meeting off an hour before it started.

3. Could you pick the children up at four?

4. Write the address down before you forget it.

5. They threw the old sofa away.

6. I looked the new word up in a dictionary.

7. Switch the lights off when you leave.

8. He handed his notice in on Monday.

9. We put the decision off until March.

10. The teacher gave the exam papers out.

Every one of the ten lines above is equally correct with the object moved to the end, after the small word. That is precisely what separable means: both positions are available, and with a noun object neither one is more correct than the other. Replace any of those objects with a pronoun, though, and only the middle position survives, which is where you will spend most of your time, since pronouns are far more frequent in real speech than full noun phrases are. Notice too how short every object in the group is: length decides which of the two orders sounds better, as the section below explains.

Inseparable phrasal verbs: the ones that never split

The question learners ask most often is which phrasal verbs cannot be separated. The honest answer is not a list to memorise but a structure to recognise: where the small word is a preposition, the object must follow it, and no exception is coming.

1. We came across an old photograph in the attic.

2. She looks after her neighbour’s cat every summer.

3. The committee looked into the complaint.

4. He takes after his mother.

5. They are dealing with the problem this week.

6. She got over the illness slowly.

7. I am waiting for the examination results.

8. The report calls for a change in the law.

In all eight lines above the object sits directly after the small word, and it stays there when you swap it for a pronoun. There is no middle position to argue about. These verbs take an object all the same; they simply refuse to let anything come between the verb and the preposition. Put the object in the middle of any of the eight and the result is not merely unusual English; it is not English at all.

Compare the two numbered groups and the difference stops being a matter of memory. The first takes a particle, so the object may go on either side of it. The second takes a preposition, so the object has exactly one place to be. Everything else about separable and inseparable phrasal verbs follows from that one contrast.

Weight decides the rest

Even when splitting is allowed, it is not always the better choice. What decides it is how heavy the object is.

She turned off the light.

She turned the light off.

She turned off every light on the ground floor of the freezing old house.

The first two lines above are short, and either arrangement sounds fine. The third carries a long object with modifiers trailing behind it, and splitting the verb around all of that would leave the listener holding an unfinished verb for a dozen words before the small word finally arrives. So the same verb, with no change in its grammar, prefers different orders depending on the weight of what follows. This is why real usage sometimes contradicts the lists you were given, and why a rule about structure serves you better than a rule about individual verbs.

Three-word verbs settle it for you

Some of these verbs come with a third element, and those are the easiest of all.

I am looking forward to it.

She puts up with a lot.

The last element in each of the two lines above is a preposition, so the object always comes at the very end, pronoun or not. Nothing ever goes in the middle. One more warning: the same pair of words can be a splitting combination with one meaning and a non-splitting one with another, so the question is never really about the verb as a dictionary item. Run the pronoun test on the sentence in front of you and it will answer for that sentence.

Register: when a single-word verb is the better choice

Phrasal verbs dominate speech and informal writing. In an examination essay or a formal report, many of them have a single-word equivalent that lifts the register, and choosing between the two is a separate skill from placing the object correctly. Getting the word order right is not the same as deciding that this was the right verb for the context. The reference page pairing these verbs with their single-word formal twins sets the two columns side by side, which is the quickest way to see what a piece of writing gains and loses by the swap.

How to learn phrasal verbs without memorising two lists

The lists in most books run to several hundred entries, and very few learners reach the end of one. A better use of your time is to learn each new phrasal verb inside a complete sentence with its object already in place, so that the word order arrives attached to the meaning instead of as a separate rule to recall later. When you meet an unfamiliar one, ask three questions: does it take an object at all; if it does, can a pronoun sit in the middle; and does the combination mean something the separate words do not.

Then produce them. Recognising a phrasal verb on a page is easy and using it correctly under time pressure is hard, so an exercise that forces you to place the object yourself is worth more than any amount of reading about the rule. That is the gap the practice set linked below is built to close.

Where to take this next

The lesson on where the small word goes in a two-part verb sets out the pattern with more cases, and the practice set that drills pronoun placement is the one to repeat until the middle position stops feeling like a decision. For a single verb that generates dozens of these combinations, the reference page that collects them is worth a slow read, and the entry for the two-part verb meaning to leave something for a later time shows how one of them behaves in real sentences. The entry for the item meaning to produce an idea, a plan or an answer is a useful second example of how one of these behaves once you meet it in a sentence.

title: How to use English idioms correctly: what to learn, and what only to recognise

fields.body:
Somewhere around the upper-intermediate level, learners are told that idioms separate a competent speaker from a natural one, and they start collecting them. The advice has the direction of travel backwards. Idioms are overwhelmingly a receptive skill, and treating them as a production target is a reliable way to make advanced English sound less natural, not more.

What an idiomatic expression actually is

An idiom is a fixed group of words whose meaning cannot be worked out by adding up the meanings of the words in it. That is the whole definition, and it has two consequences that matter more than any list. First, because the meaning is not built from the parts, it has to be stored whole, like a single item of vocabulary. Second, because it is stored whole, its form is frozen: the words, their order, their number and the small grammatical words between them are all part of the stored item rather than choices you get to make.

This is what separates an idiom from a collocation, which learners often meet under the same heading. A collocation is simply the partner word that a noun or verb ordinarily takes, and its meaning is exactly the sum of its parts. Both need to be learnt as units, but only one of them will produce a sentence that stops meaning anything if you change a single word.

Common English idioms, and what they mean

Here is a set you will meet early and often in English. Read them as recognition vocabulary: the aim on a first pass is to understand each one instantly when it arrives, not to start using it.

The exam itself was a piece of cake.

We are back to the drawing board on the pricing.

I heard it straight from the horse’s mouth.

The ball is in their court now.

The first line says that something was very easy. The second says that a plan has failed and the work must start again from the beginning; it is neutral in register and common in professional speech. The third says that the information came directly from the person who would actually know, rather than second hand. The fourth says that responsibility for the next move has passed to the other party, and it is the most useful of the four in a work context, because it states in six words a situation that otherwise takes a full sentence to set out.

They cut corners to hit the deadline.

Let me keep you in the loop.

We are all on the same page about the budget.

That is a grey area in the contract.

These four belong to ordinary professional English rather than to comedy or sport, which is what makes them safer than most. The first accuses someone of saving time or money by skipping necessary steps, and it is a genuine criticism, not a neutral observation. The second promises to keep someone informed as a situation develops. The third says that a group shares the same understanding, and it is probably the most frequent of all of them in meetings. The fourth names a case the rules do not clearly cover. Note that only the first carries a judgement; the rest are descriptive, and that difference matters more than the metaphors they are built on.

Sets like this are worth reading through in one sitting and then meeting again in context. The reference table of the expressions you will hear first lays out more of them with the situations they belong to, and the lesson on why these expressions cannot be edited explains what happens when the frozen wording is disturbed.

A misfired idiom is louder than plain language

Accurate plain English is invisible. An idiom is not: it announces itself, and the listener’s attention lands on it. That is fine when it works and expensive when it does not, because fixed expressions tolerate almost no variation. Change the preposition, put the noun in the singular, swap the animal for a closely related animal, and the phrase does not become a slightly unusual version of itself. It stops being English.

They moved the goalposts halfway through the project.

They moved the goalpost halfway through the project.

The second sentence above differs from the first by a single letter, and it is not a variant. A listener hears an error, and that error is more conspicuous than anything the speaker would have produced by describing the situation plainly. Hence the asymmetry: getting an idiom right buys little, because nobody notices ordinary fluency, and getting one wrong produces a sentence the room remembers.

Register, and whether idioms belong in formal writing

Idiom collections are assembled from books, films and comedy, so they over-represent informal, regional and dated language. An expression a British colleague finds warmly familiar can sound archaic in a meeting in Singapore, and a metaphor borrowed from a sport half the room has never watched is not shared ground but a small demand on the listener.

In formal writing the answer is close to a rule. Academic essays, legal documents, reports and examination writing all reward precision, and a figurative expression is by definition less precise than the plain statement underneath it. Examiners in particular are marking the range and accuracy of your language, and an idiom that is slightly off costs more than the plain version would ever have earned. In a professional email the line is softer: the descriptive expressions from the second set above pass easily, while anything comic, regional or ironic does not.

Irony compounds the problem. Many of the most-taught expressions are sarcastic, and sarcasm in a second language, delivered without the intonation native speakers use to mark it, is heard as sincere. The expression for an outcome that disappoints while surprising nobody is the clean example: understand it instantly when it is said to you, and never reach for it in a client call, where a listener who misses the irony hears you calling their work predictable.

What actually makes advanced speech sound fluent

Two things, and neither is glamorous: collocation, meaning the ordinary partner word a noun or verb expects, and two-part verbs. Both are far more frequent in real conversation than figurative expressions. Someone who picks the expected partner word every time and handles two-part verbs without hesitating sounds close to native with almost no figurative language, while someone with fifty memorised idioms and unstable collocation sounds like someone reciting. The two-part combinations built on the busiest verb in the language will do more for how you sound than any collection of metaphors.

A filter for the short list worth saying

An expression is worth producing, not merely understanding, when it passes three tests at once.

  • Its form is stable in your memory. You have heard it several times with the same words in the same order.
  • Its register is neutral or professional. It would not startle anyone in a meeting, and it does not depend on a shared cultural reference.
  • You could say the same thing plainly if it failed. If the expression is your only route to that meaning, you are not using an idiom, you are depending on one.

We can leverage the contract we already have.

She’s sitting on the fence until the numbers come in.

Well, that’s a surprise to absolutely nobody.

The first sentence above contains no idiom at all. It uses the plain business verb for turning something you already own into an advantage: overused, perhaps, but hard to get wrong, because it has no fixed form to break. The second is the expression for refusing to take a side: stable in form, neutral in speech, mildly informal on paper, so it passes the filter for a conversation and fails it for a report. The third is the ironic one, and it belongs in your listening vocabulary only.

The expression for changing the rules once the process has started is the strongest candidate here for active use: fixed in wording, widely known, ordinary professional register, and carrying a specific complaint that would take a full clause to state plainly. That combination is rarer than it sounds, which is the real point.

How many should you actually learn

The honest numbers are lopsided. The expressions worth recognising run into the thousands, and there is no upper limit worth setting, because recognition costs you nothing and every one you know removes a possible moment of confusion. The expressions worth producing number in the dozens, and for most learners a working set of twenty or thirty, drawn from their own field, covers everything they will ever need.

So split the effort. Recognition has no downside: let it be broad, and let it come from listening rather than lists, so the meaning arrives with the tone and the situation attached. Production should be narrow, drawn only from expressions you have heard used by people in your own field, in the kind of conversation you actually have. The vocabulary section is organised around meanings rather than word lists for exactly this reason, and the page that groups everything by subject will take you to the rest.
