title: How to write a polite email in English that does not read as rude

fields.body:
You rewrote the message three times: an apology at the top, another before the request, a closing line hoping you have not caused trouble. The reply comes back in six words and feels cold. Nothing you wrote was wrong, which is why the problem is hard to see. In English work email, politeness is carried by the shape of the request, not by the softening piled around it.

Buying politeness with length is not irrational; it works in plenty of languages, where elaboration is itself a sign of respect. In English business writing it produces a message that is expensive to read: your colleague scans for the request, cannot find it in three lines, and leaves it for later. The cost of your caution is paid by the reader.

What follows is the whole shape of a professional email in English, from the subject line down to the signature, with the three or four places marked out where politeness is actually decided. Most of the format is convention and can be learned once. Only a small part of it is yours to compose, and that is where the effort belongs.

What a formal email in English is made of

The correct format for formal emails is stable enough to be worth memorising, because a reader who recognises the structure can find what they need without reading every word. There are seven parts: a subject line, a greeting, an opening line giving the reason for writing, the body of your email in one to three short paragraphs, the request itself, a closing line, and a sign-off above your signature block.

Beyond the parts themselves, the rules for writing formal emails in English are few and mostly mechanical. Keep one subject per message, so the reader can file it and so a reply cannot answer half of it. Put the request in the top half, above the point where a phone screen ends. Use short paragraphs. Check that anything described as attached is attached, since the correction email costs both of you more than the ten seconds of checking.

Email etiquette in English is thinner than in many languages. There are fewer fixed formulas to master, and correspondingly more weight falls on the structure and on the wording of the request. That is good news for a learner: an email structure can be learned in an afternoon and reused for years, while a repertoire of ornamental phrases takes far longer to build and does less work when it is finished.

The subject line does more work than you think

A subject line is read in a list of forty others, often on a phone, by someone deciding what to open now and what to leave until later. Naming the topic is not enough. Name the topic and the decision you want, and the person about to read your email can estimate how long the message will take. That estimate is the first courtesy you offer, and it is offered before a single polite word has been used.

Question

Budget slide: Q3 figures needed by Wednesday

Application for the position of Logistics Coordinator

The first of the three subject lines above could belong to any message in the folder, so it is filed under later. The second names a document, an action and a date; the third names a role and a purpose. Neither of them is impolite for being specific. Specificity is precisely what allows a busy reader to be generous with you.

How to start a professional email politely

A formal greeting in English is shorter than most learners expect and carries less feeling than the equivalent line in their own language. It marks the point at which the message begins; it is not a place to build a relationship. The title-plus-surname form is the safe default with someone you have not met, and the bare first name becomes normal the moment they have used yours.

If you do not know the name of the person you are writing to, spend two minutes finding it before falling back on an impersonal formula. Those formulas are not rude, but they announce that nobody was looked up, and on a job application that is the first thing a hiring manager notices. Getting the name right makes a good impression before the message has said anything at all. A professional email that opens with the wrong greeting is not ruined, but it begins by telling the reader you were guessing.

Dear Ms Novak,

Dear Sir or Madam,

To whom it may concern,

Hi Marek,

The four openings above run from most formal to least, and each takes a comma. The first is the proper greeting whenever you have a name. The second and third are the impersonal fall-backs; the third is the most distant of them all and is best kept for an application sent into a system rather than to a person. The fourth is not casual in a British office, merely current: it is what colleagues write to one another all day, including upwards.

The line after the greeting should state the reason for your email inside its first sentence. Learners often spend that line praising the recipient or apologising for the interruption, which delays the only information the reader wants. Warmth is not forbidden, but it works better attached to something real than offered as a compliment.

I am writing to ask whether the March figures are final.

Thank you for sending the draft yesterday. I have one question about section three.

Both opening lines above give the reason for writing immediately. The first is the neutral formal choice and can begin almost any message to a stranger. The second is warmer, and it earns that warmth by referring to something the reader actually did rather than by describing them as busy or important. The collection of ready-made opening and closing lines has more of both kinds.

The four parts that actually carry politeness

A request that lands well in English contains four things, and none of them is an apology. It is shaped as a question, not an instruction. It uses a modal verb that grammatically permits refusal, so the reader is asked whether something is possible rather than told it will happen. It gives a reason, however short. And it names a date.

Send me the figures before the meeting.

Could you send me the figures before Thursday’s meeting? I need them for the budget slide.

The second version above is a sentence longer, and that is not why it is more polite. The verb form leaves the reader somewhere to stand, and the reason tells them what depends on their answer. Adding a courtesy word to either end of the first version would not create that room.

Naming a deadline is polite, not pushy

This is the point that most surprises learners taught that indirectness equals respect. In an English-speaking office, vagueness about timing is not consideration but a transfer of work: a reader who is not told when something is needed has to guess, and guessing wrong costs them more than being told plainly.

Let me know when you get a chance.

Could you let me know by Friday afternoon? If that’s difficult, say so and I’ll move things around.

The second message above is more demanding on paper and far more comfortable in practice. It sets a date and hands back the right to renegotiate it, and that combination reads as respect. The first looks gentler while making the reader responsible for a decision that was yours to take. Its closing half is the pattern for real conditions and their results doing ordinary work.

Two habits that travel badly

The first is the command softened only by a courtesy word. English does use imperatives politely, but for cheap actions: inviting a reply, offering help, telling someone they may refuse. Used to hand over work, the same form assigns a task, and a courtesy word tacked on the end can sharpen it rather than soften it.

The second is self-deprecation. A message that apologises for existing, calls its own request tiny and unimportant, and predicts that the reader is far too busy does not read as modest to an English-speaking manager. It reads as doubt about whether the request is legitimate, and if the writer is unsure, the reader will be too.

Send the report by tonight, please.

Sorry to bother you again, I know you’re extremely busy, it’s not urgent at all, but if you happen to have a moment, maybe you could possibly take a quick look at the report?

Could you look at the report today? I’d like to send it out tomorrow morning.

Of the three messages above, only the last tells the reader what is wanted, when, and why. The middle one spends more than twice as many words saying less, and leaves the reader unsure whether refusing is allowed or dropping everything is expected. The first is short, which is not the same as clear: it never asks.

How to end a professional email politely

The end of the message has three parts: a closing line, a sign-off and a signature block. Only the first is written fresh each time. Learners tend to compose an elaborate closing line and then choose the sign-off at random, when the attention is better spent the other way round.

A polite closing earns its place by doing one of three things: saying what you will do next, saying what you hope the reader will do, or explicitly giving them room to say no. Anything that does none of the three is decoration, and decoration at the end of a message is where a reply goes to be forgotten.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Please let me know if Wednesday is difficult and I will move the meeting.

Please don’t hesitate to let me know if you would like the longer version.

Best regards,

Yours sincerely,

The first three lines above are closing lines and the last two are sign-offs, and a message needs one of each. Of the closing lines, the first is the most formal and the emptiest; choose it only when there is genuinely nothing to add. The other two are stronger because each hands something back to the reader. Every sign-off takes a comma after the closing formula, and the last one above is the British pairing for a message that opened with the recipient’s name; its partner form belongs above an impersonal greeting instead.

What belongs in a professional email signature

A signature block is not a small advertisement. It answers the three questions a stranger would otherwise have to ask: who you are, what you do, and how else you can be reached. Your name, your job title, your company name and one telephone number is the whole of it.

Marta Reis

Logistics Coordinator, Novapak Ltd

+44 20 7946 0102

The block above is three lines long. The job title is there so the reader knows what you are able to decide; the company name is there because your address may not make it obvious; the number is there for the one message in fifty that should have been a telephone call. If you use two email addresses, say which of them you read, or the reader will guess and guess wrong.

A full example of a good formal email

Here is one message with every part in place. It asks for something the recipient may not want to give, gives a reason, names a date and leaves the door open, and it is considerably shorter than the apologetic version most learners would send.

Subject: Q3 figures for Thursday’s budget review

Dear Ms Novak,

I am writing about the budget review on Thursday. Could you send me the Q3 figures before Wednesday evening? I need them for the final slide and would rather not present an estimate.

If Wednesday is difficult, please let me know and I will ask for that slide to be taken last.

Thank you for your help.

Best regards,

Marta Reis

Logistics Coordinator, Novapak Ltd

Read that example against the four parts described earlier and all of them are there, inside two short paragraphs: a question rather than an instruction, a modal verb that permits refusal, a reason, and a date. The fourth line offers a way out that costs the writer very little. Nothing in the message apologises and nothing in it is blunt, and that combination is what an English-speaking reader means when they call an email good.

Formal, neutral and informal are three settings, not two

Register is set by vocabulary and sentence length far more than by politeness formulas. A message to a regulator, a message to a client of two years’ standing and a message to the colleague at the next desk share one structure and use three different vocabularies. Always selecting the most formal language is not the safe choice it appears to be: to someone you see daily it reads as distance, and unexplained distance in an informal email reads as displeasure.

The most economical way to raise the register is to replace two-part verbs with their single-word equivalents, and the table of two-part verbs and their formal twins is the shortest route to that habit. Travelling in the other direction, towards a neutral business email, the two-part verb is usually the more natural of the pair.

Could you sort out the delivery problem before Friday?

Could you resolve the delivery issue before Friday?

Both requests above are polite and both are correct. The first belongs in a message to someone you speak to every day; the second belongs in a message that may be forwarded to a client. The grammar is identical. Only the two words in the middle have changed, and a professional tone in English is produced by that kind of precision rather than by ornament.

Best practices that genuinely improve email writing

Email writing skills improve the way every other second-language skill improves: by reducing the number of decisions made from scratch. An email template you have built yourself, with the seven parts marked and two or three versions of each line, removes most of them. A template downloaded from elsewhere does much less, because its phrases were chosen for somebody else’s situation and you cannot tell which of them are load-bearing.

Three habits do the remaining work. Write the request first and add the courtesies afterwards, so the message is built around the thing it exists for. Keep to short paragraphs of about three sentences, because a wall of text reads as urgency whatever the words say. And read the finished message once as though you were the person receiving it late on a Friday; the sentences that survive that reading have earned their place.

The hardest of these messages is the one that says no. The exercise on refusing a request without causing offence is worth working through before you need it rather than after.

What to keep and what to cut

None of this argues for bluntness. Softening belongs in the opening and closing lines, where it costs the reader nothing, rather than wrapped around the request, where it hides the one thing they were looking for.

If you write these messages daily, work through the lesson on asking for things politely at work until the four-part shape is automatic, and keep the ready-made opening and closing lines beside you until it is. To explain who else is waiting, English has a single noun for anyone with an interest in how something turns out, and it replaces a whole clause. The reference section collects the other patterns worth keeping within reach.

The rule of thumb is short: cut every sentence whose only content is that you feel bad about writing, and keep the question, the reason and the date.
fields.excerpt: Politeness in a professional email in English is carried by the shape of the request. The format, the phrases and the habits that make formal emails land well.

title: Singular opener, plural noun: the grammar rule your course left out

fields.body:
In your first weeks of English you met a pair of openers for saying that something exists: one shape for a single thing, another shape for several. The rule is easy to state and easy to drill. Then you watch a film, and within ten minutes a character uses the singular shape in front of an obviously plural noun, and nobody in the room reacts. If you have quietly wondered whether your textbook lied to you, it did not. It left something out.

The rule is real, and it is the one to learn

Here is what your course teaches, in its two shapes.

There is a problem with the booking.

There are two problems with the booking.

The verb agrees with the noun that follows it, exactly as verbs agree everywhere else in the language. Nothing about this construction is special in careful writing, and the second line above is the shape you want whenever you mean more than one thing. That is worth saying plainly before anything else, because the rest of this page is about the moments when your ears will tell you otherwise, and about the one place further down where the rule itself bends.

One point of English grammar is worth making before the examples multiply. The word that opens both example sentences above is not really doing its ordinary job. Elsewhere in the English language it is an adverb that refers to a specific place; here it refers to nothing at all. It is a placeholder that fills the subject slot so the sentence can begin, while the real subject waits behind the verb. The whole construction exists in order to say that something exists, and it holds the thing back until after the verb. That is why the verb takes its grammatical number from what follows rather than from what precedes it: the noun behind it is the thing being announced, and the opening word means nothing on its own.

What you are actually hearing

In speech, the singular opener turns up in front of plural nouns constantly, in every major variety of English, from every kind of speaker. It is not regional, it is not carelessness, and it is not a sign of poor education. Listen for it in the next thing you watch and you will catch it within a few minutes.

There’s two buses an hour.

There’s a lot of people waiting outside.

Notice what both lines above have in common: the verb is contracted onto the word in front of it. That is the whole explanation. Once it is shortened and attached, speakers stop processing it as a verb at all. It becomes a single fixed chunk whose job is to announce that something is about to be mentioned, and a chunk does not agree with anything. The full, unshortened singular form in front of a plural noun is much rarer, because there the verb is still audible as a verb and speakers feel the clash. The plural form can be contracted too, but the result is awkward to say and almost never written, which leaves the singular chunk covering both jobs.

It reaches informal writing as well, wherever people write the way they talk: messages, comments, captions, anything typed quickly. What you will not often find is the same chunk in edited prose, because an editor generally takes it out. Usage guides have objected to it for well over a century without denting it at all, which tells you how firmly it sits in the spoken language.

Recognise it; do not produce it

So the honest answer splits in two. As a listener, treat it as a fact about spoken English: when it goes past you, nothing has gone wrong, you have not misheard, and your grammar is not out of date. Nobody explains this in a beginner classroom, which is exactly why it unsettles the learners who are otherwise doing well.

Your own output is a different matter. Editors correct it, teachers mark it, and examiners count it under grammatical accuracy in both writing and speaking. Copying it buys you nothing: the plural form costs you one extra syllable and nothing else. And there is an unfairness you should simply plan around: a form that passes unnoticed from a fluent speaker is read as an error when it comes from a learner. That is unfair, and it is also how it works.

A quick test, then, before you send anything that matters. Imagine the sentence read aloud by a newsreader rather than by a friend. If the newsreader version is the one you want, use the full plural form. Producing it correctly is free: formal writing has no tolerance for the spoken chunk, and no reader has ever complained that the longer form was too long.

The case your textbook skipped

One situation is genuinely different, and no beginner course mentions it: a list.

There is a knife and two forks in the drawer.

There are two forks and a knife in the drawer.

Both lines above are normal, and the only difference between them is which item comes first. When a list follows the opener, the verb agrees with the item nearest to it rather than with the total, so a single first item pulls the singular verb even though the drawer holds three things. Reverse the order, as in the second line, and the verb turns plural. This is not a spoken shortcut and not a modern slip; careful writers have done it for centuries. Your course leaves it out because it complicates a rule that beginners need to install first.

Questions and negatives: the grammar does not change

Most ESL courses install the two positive shapes in the first term and never come back to them. Learners who have drilled those shapes then lose the distinction the moment the sentence stops being a plain statement. It should not happen, because forming a question or a negative changes the word order, not the agreement.

Is there a problem with the booking?

Are there two problems with the booking?

There is not a problem with the booking.

There are not any problems with the booking.

In the first two lines above the verb simply hops in front of the opening word. Everything else stays where it was, and the noun still decides which form of the verb you need. In the last two the negative attaches to the verb instead, and again you look past it to the noun to know which form to use. One extra habit is visible in the final line: after a plural negative, English usually prefers the non-specific determiner to a bare number word. That small choice is worth copying, because getting it right is most of what makes a negative sound native.

Singular or plural: which noun the verb is listening to

Agreeing with the following noun is easy advice to give when the noun is a plain countable one. It stops being easy when the noun belongs to a type your first course never sorted out.

There is a lot of traffic on the ring road.

There are three chairs in the waiting room.

There is a team of engineers on site.

There are six children in the group.

The first line above contains an uncountable noun. Nouns of that type have no plural form and cannot be counted one by one, so you use the singular verb with them however much of the stuff you are describing. The second line is the plain countable case, behaving exactly as your course promised. The third holds a collective noun, a single word naming a group of people; British English allows either verb with these, depending on whether you mean the group acting as one body or its members acting separately, but after this particular opener the singular is far more common and it is the safer choice in an exam.

The fourth line is the one that catches people out. Its noun is plural, but it does not end in the letter that normally marks a plural, so learners read it as singular and reach for the wrong verb. Irregular plurals do this constantly, and they are common enough in everyday speech that you cannot route around them. If that group of nouns still slows you down, the reference page on plural forms that refuse to follow the rule is where to fix it.

Quantity phrases that hide the real noun

Easily the most common source of error at intermediate level is a quantity phrase sitting between the opener and the noun. The phrase looks like the subject, so learners agree the verb with it, and the sentence comes out wrong.

There are a lot of people waiting outside.

There is a lot of noise in the corridor.

There are plenty of seats left.

There is plenty of room left.

The quantity phrase is identical across the first pair of lines above, and identical again across the second pair. What changes each time is the noun at the end of it, and that noun is what the verb answers to. If you can count the thing, use the plural verb; if you can only measure it, use the singular. The phrase in the middle never decides, however long it grows, and a phrase of four or five words is exactly where a careful learner loses track.

Past, future and perfect: the same choice in other tenses

Nothing about this pattern is locked to the present. Move the verb into another tense and the construction carries over unchanged, still taking its number from the noun that follows it. Only the conjugation of the verb changes.

There was a mistake in the invoice.

There were three mistakes in the invoice.

There will be a meeting on Thursday.

There have been complaints about the noise.

The first two lines above move the choice into the past, where it works exactly as it does in the present: one form for a single thing, another for many. The third line is the easy case. Once a modal joins in, the main verb has only one form left, so the singular and plural question disappears and a single shape covers both. The fourth line brings the choice back: in the perfect it is the auxiliary in front that changes with the noun, even though the participle behind it never does.

Confused words: three spellings, one sound

One further confusion is worth clearing up, because it costs marks in writing rather than in speaking. The word that opens every example on this page has two homophones: a possessive determiner, and a pronoun with a contracted verb attached. All three sound identical when spoken, and a spellchecker will not help you, because each of them is a real English word in its own right. They are among the most confused words in the language, and the other two words have nothing to do with existence at all.

There are two boxes by the door.

Their boxes are by the door.

They’re leaving the boxes by the door.

Only the first line above is the existence construction under discussion here. The second opens with a possessive determiner and tells you whose the boxes are; the third opens with a pronoun and a contracted verb and tells you what somebody is doing. Learners rarely confuse the three meanings. They confuse the three spellings, under time pressure, in an exam, and the mark is lost anyway. If that trio is a habitual slip of yours, the reference page on words that trap even native writers is the drill that clears it.

What to do this week

Install the agreement rule properly for your own use. The lesson on saying that something exists lays out both shapes with their question and negative forms, and the practice set that makes you choose between one thing and many is worth ten minutes a day until the choice stops costing you any thought. If it is the verb itself that slows you down rather than the choice, keep the reference page for the three present forms of the language’s most important verb open beside you. Mastering the choice is a fortnight of short sessions, not a term of study.

Then stop grading what you hear against what you write. Understanding and producing are separate skills at every stage, and they are allowed to disagree; the page that sorts everything here by level is built on exactly that assumption.
fields.excerpt: The singular opener turns up before plural nouns in every kind of English speech. Here is why it happens, when the rule genuinely bends, and what to write.

title: Pronunciation of the regular past ending: three sounds, one rule

fields.body:
Almost every course teaches the pronunciation of the regular past ending as three lists to memorise: verbs that take one sound, verbs that take another, verbs that gain a whole extra syllable. Three lists is the wrong shape for this problem. There is only one decision, your mouth already knows how to make it, and the reason learners keep getting it wrong is that they are looking at the wrong thing.

The three sounds, and the one question that chooses between them

The past tense ending on regular verbs is pronounced in three different ways in English. Two of them are single consonant sounds that add nothing to the length of the word; the third adds an extra syllable. Which one you pronounce is decided entirely by the final sound of the verb in front of the ending, and by nothing else.

She walked home.

She played tennis.

She waited outside.

Put two fingers on your throat and pronounce the last sound of each verb above, stopping before the ending. On the first line your vocal cords are silent: that final sound is voiceless, sometimes called unvoiced. On the second they are already vibrating, because a vowel sound is always voiced. That vibration, or its absence, is the entire rule. The ending simply continues whatever the sound before it was doing: voiceless before, voiceless ending; voiced before, voiced ending. You are not choosing between two sounds, you are letting the ending copy its neighbour, which is what your mouth wants to do anyway.

After a voiceless consonant

When the verb ends in a voiceless consonant sound, the vocal cords are switched off as you arrive at the ending, and they stay off. There is no vibration to carry over, and no syllable is added.

He stopped the car.

She kissed her mother.

They washed the windows.

We watched the news.

After a voiced consonant, or any vowel

When the verb ends in a voiced consonant sound, or in any vowel sound at all, the vocal cords are already running and simply keep going through the ending. Again no syllable is added, and the word is exactly as long as it was before.

She called her sister.

He opened the door.

They cleaned the kitchen.

We agreed on a price.

Only two sounds add a syllable

Exactly two sounds in the whole language force the extra syllable: the voiceless and voiced pair made by tapping the tongue just behind the top teeth. Those are the two sounds the ending itself is built from, so when a verb already finishes with one of them the ending would be inaudible unless a small vowel came in to separate them. That is all the extra syllable is doing.

The meeting started late.

They decided to wait.

He needed more time.

She counted the votes.

Every one of the four verbs above gains a beat, and every regular verb outside that narrow group keeps exactly the number of syllables it had before. So the extra syllable is the rare case, not the default. If your first language does not allow consonant clusters at the end of a word, you will be tempted to insert that little vowel everywhere, and that single habit is the most audible marker of a learner accent in past tense storytelling, more noticeable in practice than a grammar slip.

An easy way to remember it

Do not memorise which verbs belong to which list. Ask one question instead: is my throat vibrating on the sound immediately before the ending? If the verb already ends in the tapping sound the ending is made of, you get the extra syllable. Otherwise the ending copies its neighbour, voiced for voiced and voiceless for voiceless. One question, asked in the time it takes to say the verb, replaces all three lists.

Spelling will lie to you

Here is the part that catches careful students hardest. The rule is about sound, and only about sound. Learners who reason from the written form look at the last letter, which is not the same as the last sound, and go wrong on exactly the verbs they were being careful about.

He laughed at the idea.

They danced until midnight.

The committee judged the entries.

In the first sentence above, two written letters combine into a single voiceless sound before the ending, so the ending is voiceless. In the second, the letter before the ending is not pronounced the way that letter usually is, and the sound it actually makes is voiceless too. In the third, the letters spell a voiced sound, so the ending is voiced. Not one of the three can be settled by the last letter you see. The silent letter that many verbs carry at the end of their base form is irrelevant for the same reason: it is not a sound, so it decides nothing about what follows it. The reference page on letters that are written but never said is worth a look if those forms are slowing you down.

The same logic, incidentally, governs the plural ending on nouns and the ending that appears on the verb when someone else is acting: copy the voicing of the sound before, and add a syllable only when that sound is too close to the ending to be heard beside it. A wider set of sounds triggers the extra syllable there, so carry the principle across, not the two-sound list.

The exceptions nobody teaches

A small set of words keeps the extra syllable when they work as adjectives, even though the matching verb does not.

He learned the trick in an afternoon.

She is a learned woman.

The priest blessed the crowd.

They sat in blessed silence.

The first and third lines above follow the ordinary rule and gain nothing. In the second and fourth, the identical written word carries an extra beat because it has stopped being a verb and become an adjective. A handful of other adjectives behave the same way and have no everyday verb standing beside them at all.

a wretched night

a crooked line

an aged cheese

the naked eye

Each of the four above is two syllables where you might expect one. The set is closed and somewhat literary in tone, so treat these as vocabulary to be learnt one at a time rather than as a pattern to apply.

How to practise it

Do not sort verbs into lists. Say them aloud, feel the throat, and let the ending follow. Record yourself telling a short story about yesterday and listen back for the little vowel you did not mean to insert; it is far easier to hear in your own recording than in the moment. The lesson that walks through the three endings one at a time gives you the sounds slowly, and the listening set that asks which ending you just heard is the fastest way to prove you can now hear the difference. If the written forms are still slowing you down, the lesson on building the regular past covers the spelling side, and the list of verbs that never take this ending at all saves you from applying the rule where it does not belong. Everything else is sorted on the page that groups lessons by subject.

title: Paraphrasing the question in IELTS Writing Task 2: what examiners reward

fields.body:
Every exam site tells you to rewrite the task statement in your own words, so consistently that candidates treat it as a rule of the exam. It is not. Open the public band descriptors for the IELTS writing paper, or the criteria for the Cambridge exams: paraphrasing is named nowhere. What is named is your response to the task, the organisation of your ideas, your vocabulary and your grammar. That does not make the advice worthless. It makes it a means to an end, worth doing only when it serves one of the four things that are actually scored, and worth abandoning when it does not.

What paraphrasing means in IELTS Writing Task 2

To paraphrase is to restate something so that the wording changes and the meaning does not. In IELTS Writing Task 2 the thing being restated is the essay prompt: a statement of a position or a situation, followed by an instruction line telling you what to do with it. The paraphrase belongs at the top of the introduction, ahead of the thesis statement in which you state your own view.

Only two kinds of change are available. You can replace words with near-equivalents, or you can keep the words and rebuild the sentence structure around them. Most candidates use the first almost exclusively, and it is the one that goes wrong. The second is where the marks sit, because grammatical range is a criterion in its own right and a restructured sentence is direct evidence of it.

Why the advice exists anyway

Two honest reasons sit behind it, and neither is the one usually given. The first is administrative: in the IELTS test, words copied straight from the question paper are discounted against the minimum length. Write 250 words of which forty came from the prompt, and you have written 210 countable words, with the penalty that follows a short answer.

The second is that vocabulary is scored on range and precision, and a good paraphrase is cheap evidence of both, placed where the examiner starts reading. But an inaccurate paraphrase is not neutral: it is evidence in the other direction, on two criteria at once.

A third reason is real but rarely stated. Paraphrasing a prompt forces you to read it slowly. Candidates who copy the question paper word for word into the introduction have often not yet worked out what the instruction line asks for, and the essay drifts from the second paragraph onwards. The paraphrase is a comprehension check disguised as a stylistic flourish, and that is the most useful thing about it.

Where it costs marks

The criterion asking whether you answered the question set carries the same weight as the other three, and it is the only one a misread prompt can wreck outright. A paraphrase that shifts the meaning changes the question you answer, and every paragraph after it is off target. Prompt wording limits the scope of the task, and those limiting words are exactly the ones candidates swap under pressure.

Some people believe that governments should spend more on public transport than on new roads.

Many think the state must stop funding roads and pay only for buses and trains.

Some argue that public money should favour public transport over road building.

The second line above is a fluent paraphrase that has quietly changed the task. A question about which of two things deserves more money has become one about abolishing one of them, and a claim about two kinds of vehicle has appeared that the original never made. An essay answering it answers a prompt nobody set. The third line rewrites the framing and leaves the meaning untouched, which is what the technique should look like.

Three paraphrasing techniques, in order of safety

The paraphrasing techniques available to you can be ranked by how much they earn and how little they risk. Ranked that way they run in almost exactly the reverse of the order most candidates use them in.

Change the sentence structure first

Restructuring is safer than swapping words: turning an active clause into a passive one, or a heavy noun phrase into a clause, demonstrates grammatical range, a criterion in its own right, without touching the meaning. You can also move a subordinate clause from the end of the sentence to the front, split one long sentence into two, or convert a statement about people into a statement about a situation.

Many companies now expect their employees to be available outside working hours.

In many companies, employees are now expected to be available after the working day has ended.

The second line above keeps nearly every content word of the first and changes only the architecture. What was the subject has become an opening adverbial, the verb has gone into the passive, and the closing phrase has become a clause with its own verb. Nothing has been guessed at, so the original meaning survives intact and nothing can be wrong. The sentence is also more obviously the work of a candidate who controls the grammar.

Then change the word form

The second operation keeps the vocabulary and changes its grammar. A verb becomes a noun, an adjective becomes a noun, a noun becomes a modifier, and the sentence reorganises around the new part of speech. This costs less than a synonym because the root meaning travels intact; only the word form has moved, and the examiner can still see the original idea underneath it.

Governments should regulate the advertising that is aimed at children.

The regulation of advertising aimed at children should be a matter for the state.

In the second line above, the verb of the first has become the subject noun, and the body that was doing the regulating has moved to the end. The idea is untouched; only its grammatical packaging has changed. This particular move earns twice over, because turning actions into nouns is one of the standard markers of an academic register: the reference on turning actions into nouns sets out the patterns worth having automatic before test day.

Reach for a synonym last

Using synonyms comes last because it is the only operation that can silently change the meaning. A word taken from a thesaurus arrives without its collocations, its register and its usual grammatical company, and all three of those are marked. The safe rule is to use the near-equivalents you already own rather than the ones you met an hour ago.

Some people think that the best way to reduce crime is to impose longer prison sentences.

It is sometimes argued that the most effective response to crime is a longer custodial sentence.

A few individuals opine that the optimum method of decreasing criminality is elongated incarceration.

The second line above changes three items and leaves the rest alone, and each substitute keeps the company it normally keeps. The third changes everything. Every one of its substitutes can be defended from a dictionary and none survives contact with the sentence: two belong to a register the rest of the line does not share, one carries a modifier that never collocates with the noun it has been attached to, and the whole reads as a candidate displaying vocabulary rather than using it. On the very criterion it was meant to impress, the third line scores below an unedited copy of the first.

Which words need changing, and which must not

The workable rule is narrower than the advice. Rewrite what you are certain of: the framing verbs, the vague quantifiers, the clause order. Leave technical terms alone. If the prompt names a field of study, a legal concept or a technology, that term rarely has a true synonym, and the substitute you invent reads as a mistake rather than as range. Repeating a technical noun from the question is not penalised; turning it into something slightly different is.

So the short answer to whether every word of a Task 2 question has to be paraphrased is no, and attempting it is itself an error. Proper nouns stay. Numbers and dates stay. The central topic noun usually stays, because the whole essay is about it and an unsteady synonym for it will wobble through every body paragraph. What changes is the frame around it: the reporting verb, the quantifier that says how many people hold the view, the modal, and the order in which the parts arrive. Three or four confident changes are enough to make an opening sentence your own, and nobody is counting them.

The paraphrasing mistakes that cost the most

Beyond thesaurus damage, four errors recur. Copying the question paper unchanged, which is discounted from the word count and demonstrates nothing. Paraphrasing so freely that the scope of the task moves, which is the expensive one described above and the hardest to notice while you are doing it. Spending eight minutes of a forty-minute task on a single sentence, so that the final paragraph arrives unfinished or not at all. And rewriting the instruction line along with the statement, which is unnecessary work: that line tells you what to produce rather than what to discuss, and candidates who rephrase it often drop half of what it asked for.

There is a fifth, quieter one. Some candidates paraphrase so thoroughly that the examiner cannot tell whether the prompt was understood or merely processed. If a reader who has the question paper in front of them has to work to match your opening sentence to it, you have gone too far. The test of a good paraphrase is that the mapping back to the original sentence is instant and the wording is nonetheless yours.

What a paraphrase is worth on your band score

Keep the size of the prize in proportion. An IELTS essay is marked on four criteria of equal weight: how completely you answer the task, the coherence and cohesion of your organisation, the lexical range and precision of your vocabulary, and your grammar. A paraphrase can touch three of them and decide none. A paraphrased opening is one sentence out of perhaps fifteen, so on its own it cannot lift a script from one band to the next, and no introduction has ever produced a band 9 by itself.

What it can do is set the first impression, and that cuts both ways. The band 7 vocabulary descriptor asks for a range wide enough to allow some flexibility and precision, and for less common items used with some awareness of style and collocation. A well-judged paraphrase is precisely that evidence, delivered in the examiner’s first ten seconds. An overreached one is evidence of the opposite, and it is followed by an essay now read with more suspicion. The same four criteria apply to the IELTS Academic and the General Training paper, so none of this changes with the version you sit.

Different Task 2 question types need different openings

The statement in the prompt is only half of what you are answering. The instruction line decides what the introduction has to contain, and the safe opening differs with it. A task asking how far you agree needs an opening that reports the view as somebody else’s, so that your own can be attached to it. A task asking you to discuss both sides needs an opening that holds two positions in the frame, not one. A task about a problem and its remedies needs an opening that names the situation without pre-empting the solutions you are about to propose.

It is often claimed that stricter licensing would make city roads safer, and this essay largely agrees.

Opinion is divided over whether stricter licensing would make city roads any safer.

Injuries on city roads have risen steadily, and the causes lie in both licensing and road design.

The three lines above describe the same situation and answer three different instructions. The first commits to a side, which is safe only where the task asks for one. The second holds both positions open, which is what a discussion task requires and what candidates most often lose marks for skipping. The third states a problem in a way that leaves room for remedies and pre-empts none of them. Choosing the wrong one of these is not a vocabulary slip; it is an error on the criterion that decides whether you answered the question at all.

The same trap, wearing a different hat

The advice to add more linking words fails the same way. Cohesion is scored, but the mid-band descriptors identify linking that is mechanical, inaccurate or overused as a feature of a middling script. A text with a connector bolted to the front of every sentence does not read as organised, but as signalling structure instead of having it.

Moreover, the cost is very high. Furthermore, few people benefit. In addition, the scheme is unpopular.

The scheme is expensive, and the benefit reaches very few people. That is why it remains unpopular.

The first text above uses three connectors to join facts whose relationship was already obvious. The second uses one signpost and reads as an argument rather than a list; it scores higher, on the very criterion the first was trying to buy.

Good cohesion is mostly invisible: known information comes early in the sentence, new information late, and consecutive sentences keep the same subject where they can. Where a connector is genuinely needed, precision beats variety: one used for contrast where the real relation is concession is a vocabulary error wearing decoration.

What to do with your first sentence instead

If your introduction has room for one thing done well, make it a clear position rather than a clever paraphrase. The task criteria reward a stance stated early and held to the end, and no amount of synonym work rescues an answer whose position the examiner must reconstruct from the conclusion.

Give the opening sentence ninety seconds, not eight minutes. Restructure what you can restructure with confidence, shift one or two words into a different part of speech, replace only the vocabulary you would use unprompted, and move on to the argument, which is where three of the four criteria are decided.

To turn these paraphrasing skills into something that survives the pressure of the real exam, work through the lesson on rewriting the question in your own words, then the exercise on rewriting an action as a noun, which trains the word-form change until it is automatic. Then treat connectors as a precision problem: pick from the reference list of connectors by the relation you actually mean, and the exercise on choosing the right one beats memorising a longer list. If you are unsure the paper sits at your level, check the level overview first.
